summary: Thirty-four axes across every area of LLM cost, adjudicated with symmetric challenge and a quote-grep gate
logs: 28 passes x2 refuters · 48 rejections x1 advocate

axes.notes:
Scope worked: platform.claude.com/docs pricing page (raw .md fetch via curl, the Mintlify `<path>.md` suffix serves unrendered source — used this to grep exact quotes per Rule 3/5 instead of trusting WebFetch's AI-summarized HTML-to-markdown pass), the API release-notes changelog (Apr 2026–Aug 18 2026, read in full), anthropic.com/news (Aug 2026 posts — nothing billing-relevant), and three feature docs fetched and grepped directly: compaction, tool-search-tool, mid-conversation-system-messages.

WebSearch was unavailable all session (\"this session has used its web search budget (200 of 200)\" — shared across whatever else ran in this session before I started); substituted entirely with WebFetch + direct curl of platform.claude.com's raw-markdown doc mirror, which worked for every URL I tried. Nothing was left unreached because of it.

Examined and rejected as not novel / not on-axis, with reasons:
- Zero-output refusal billing (release note, June 2, 2026: \"you are no longer billed for a request when it returns stop_reason: 'refusal' without Claude having generated any output\") — exact duplicate of existing-226 entry 176 (CONTRACTUAL_ONLY). Dropped.
- Sonnet 5 introductory pricing becoming permanent (Aug 10, 2026 note) — duplicate of entry 177.
- Managed Agents session budgets (Aug 7, 2026: hard spend cap, `budget_reached` stop reason) — a spend-limit feature, not a claim that tokens/model/thinking are unchanged; also overlaps entry 126's territory (native budget alerts/hard spend caps). Doesn't map onto the FAIL/PASS taxonomy; dropped.
- Self-hosted sandboxes (Managed Agents) — read the full doc; tool execution moves to the customer's own infrastructure, but nothing on the pricing page or the sandbox doc states session-runtime billing ($0.08/session-hour) changes or is waived when execution is self-hosted (grepped pricing.md for \"self.hosted\" — zero hits). No falsifiable savings claim to test; dropped rather than guess.
- 1M-token \"long context pricing\" (\"a 900k-token request is billed at the same per-token rate as a 9k-token request\") — a flat no-premium pricing statement, not a caching/dedup mechanism with a testable \"did the model read different tokens\" question. Out of scope for the verdict taxonomy.
- Code execution \"files preloaded onto the container bill execution time even if the tool is not called\" and \"free when used with web search/fetch\" — both already covered by existing-226 entries 79/80 (FAIL); the files-preloaded nuance is a hidden-cost gotcha, not a false-savings claim, so it doesn't fit the FAIL/PASS bar either.
- Fast mode stacking rules, Sonnet 5 lacking Priority Tier, `inference_geo` 1.1x data-residency multiplier — all straightforward surcharge/tier mechanics already generally covered by entries 78/87/101/106, none framed as a savings claim under test.
- Mid-conversation tool changes itself, Admin API user-management (Jul 14), Compliance API local-session transcripts (Aug 11), `anthropic-workspace-id` header, inference hooks, MCP tunnels, Playground rename (Aug 18) — governance/product features with no billing-equivalence claim to adjudicate.

No repo/tool dependency in any candidate, so Rule 7 (verify stars/last-push) doesn't apply here — all three rest on Anthropic's own first-party docs, fetched and grepped directly today. No ANTHROPIC_API_KEY existed this session and no request was sent; every proposed verdict above is a documentation-only read, capped accordingly (CONTRACTUAL_ONLY where the docs concede the full request left the customer's machine; FAIL where the docs plainly state the token stream itself is altered, which is a mechanical fact rather than an unverifiable identity assertion).
unreachable: WebSearch tool: "this session has used its web search budget (200 of 200 WebSearch calls)" on every query attempted (Anthropic pricing changelog, Admin API pricing, 1M context pricing) — budget was already exhausted before this task started. Worked around it with WebFetch (AI-summarized) plus direct `curl` against platform.claude.com/docs/en/**/*.md (Mintlify's raw-markdown mirror), which returned full source text I could grep for Rule 3/5 compliance, so no candidate here rests on an unverified WebSearch snippet.

axes.notes:
Fetch path: openai.com/api/pricing/ returned HTTP 403 on both a default curl UA and a spoofed Chrome UA (rule 6 case) — did not guess from memory; instead found developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/* is the canonical, SSR'd (non-empty, non-shell) docs/pricing host used by openai.com's own internal links, confirmed by curl returning full prose HTML (200, 300-800KB per page) for every guide fetched. All quotes below are grepped against the tag-stripped text of these pages; raw-HTML grep was cross-checked for the submitted candidate's quote (hit count matched modulo an HTML line-wrap, not a splice).

Reviewed and NOT submitted, with reasons:
- Automatic/general prompt caching (matches dedupe #43, #82, #83, #174) — re-verified current docs still say verbatim 'Prompt Caching does not change how the model generates output tokens' and 'The model computes a new response from the cached prompt prefix' — same PASS_ABSOLUTE-grade provider assurance already logged. Not resubmitted.
- GPT-5.6's new explicit cache-breakpoint system (prompt_cache_options.mode, up to 4 breakpoints/request, 50-breakpoint read lookback) and its new 1.25x cache-write charge — genuinely new pricing/mechanics not literally in the 226 corpus, but it rests on the identical output-identity assurance already covered by #43, so judged a version update of an already-logged entry rather than a distinct novel claim. Not submitted, to avoid padding.
- Fast mode (dedupe #87, service_tier=priority|fast) — docs explicitly state 'Priority processing was renamed Fast mode on July 30, 2026,' confirming this is the same mechanism already logged. Not resubmitted.
- Flex processing (#86), Scale/Reserved Tier (#88/#89), Batch API in all its forms (#63/#69/#77/#85/#137/#138 etc.), Predicted Outputs (#90), Structured Outputs schema cache (#91), previous_response_id (#92), prompt_cache_key (#83/#174) — all reviewed via the docs nav tree; each matches an existing dedupe entry's mechanism. Not resubmitted.
- Realtime API prompt caching — same underlying caching mechanism as the general case, not separately novel.
- Realtime conversation truncation (token_limits.post_instructions, session.truncation.retention_ratio) — genuinely changes what the model reads on later turns, but OpenAI discloses the tradeoff openly in the same paragraph ('there may be a tradeoff here in terms of lower cost but lower model memory for a given turn'), so it isn't a product silently sold as unchanged — rejected as not deceptive enough to be a 'trap' finding, and mechanically similar to already-logged context-truncation entries (#157, #226).
- Realtime conversation.item.truncate (interruption handling) — changes future context (cuts unplayed audio+transcript) but I found no cost/savings claim attached to it anywhere in the Realtime docs; it's framed purely as barge-in UX. Rejected for lack of a billing-savings hook to test against the bar.
- web_search tool's external_web_access:false ('offline/cache-only mode') — no price differential vs. live search documented anywhere on the page; rejected, nothing to test.
- Code Interpreter memory tiers (1g/4g/16g/64g) — plain compute-tier pricing, not a same-product claim.
- File search 'limit number of results' — openly documented as trading tokens for 'reduced answer quality,' i.e. disclosed, not sold as free/identical; rejected.
- Moderation endpoint ('free to use') — literally free, no baseline savings claim to test.
- Fine-tuning (RFT/SFT/DPO/vision) and embeddings dimension truncation — no cost-identity claim found; embeddings dimension reduction only affects output vector size, not input tokens the model reads, so it sits outside the bar's mechanism entirely.

WebSearch tool: session's search budget was already exhausted (200/200) before I could run supplementary queries, so this sweep relied entirely on direct curl/WebFetch against developers.openai.com and platform.openai.com — no secondary corroborating web search was possible. - Gemini 3.5 Live Translate audio billed at '$0.0053/min' equivalent to 25 tokens/sec — a unit-conversion disclosure, not a savings mechanism.
- Per-frame 'media resolution' controls for image/video token cost — an overt, disclosed quality/cost dial the developer sets; not sold as identical-but-cheaper.
- File Search tool ($0.15/1M-token embeddings, retrieved-doc tokens billed as regular tokens) and Code execution / URL context ('free to invoke, tool output billed as regular tokens') on the Gemini API 'Additional usage' table — same shape as already-logged entries #79/#180/#182 (Anthropic tool-fee structure); provider-specific but lower novelty than the six submitted, so dropped rather than padding.

Dedupe file read first (226 entries, /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/existing-226.txt). AWS Bedrock is already heavily represented there: prompt caching (id 98, PASS_METADATA), batch inference (id 99, CONTRACTUAL_ONLY), Provisioned Throughput / Reserved Tier generic and Anthropic-specific (ids 100, 108, 112-113, 196-197, mix of INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE/CONTRACTUAL_ONLY/FAIL), cross-region inference Geo vs Global (id 101, CONTRACTUAL_ONLY), AWS Marketplace private offers and EDP/PPA drawdown (ids 102, 114-115, PASS_ABSOLUTE), CreateModelInvocationJob idempotency (id 36, CONTRACTUAL_ONLY), Bedrock batch conditional-write orchestration (id 39, INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE), and a third-party 'bedrockcache' audit tool (id 16, INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE). WebSearch was unavailable all session (budget exhausted at start -- '200 of 200' used before my first query ran); every finding below came from WebFetch + raw curl+grep against AWS's own pages, per the anti-splice rule, using a browser UA since AWS blocks bare curl. Fetched and read as raw HTML (not markdown) for the pricing tables per rule 5: aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/ (7,765 lines), aws.amazon.com/bedrock/model-distillation/, aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/ (3,049 lines, JSON-embedded copy). docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/.../model-import-supported-models-serving.html 404-redirected to a JS stub and was abandoned in favor of the pricing-page section on the same topic, which had the needed language.

Examined and rejected, by axis-brief topic:
- Guardrails pricing: real and quoted (content filters $0.15/1k text units, images $0.00075/image, denied topics $0.15/1k, sensitive-info filters $0.10/1k, contextual grounding $0.10/1k, Automated Reasoning checks $0.17/1k per policy) but every one of these is a flat additive per-unit charge for a new safety/verification layer, never framed as 'same thing you already had, now cheaper.' Automated Reasoning checks are symbolic/formal verification, not an LLM call, so the token/model/thinking bar doesn't even engage. Not a savings claim in the sense this register audits -- rejected.
- Knowledge Bases: index storage $5/GB/mo, standard retrieval $1/1,000 calls, agentic retrieval $4/1,000 (+$1/1,000 underlying) calls, and 'multimodal parsing, embeddings generation, and re-ranking included at no charge with managed models.' RAG retrieval overtly changes what the model reads by design (that's the product), so it isn't a hidden-substitution savings claim either. The 'no charge' bundling line is pricing info, not an equivalence claim -- rejected as below the bar's threshold for inclusion, though flagged here per the instruction to report what was looked at.
- Bedrock Marketplace (the third-party/open-model catalog, distinct from the general 'AWS Marketplace' private-offer program already covered by ids 102/114/115): confirmed via WebFetch that Marketplace-hosted models are billed per configured instance-hour with customer-defined autoscaling, not per-token and not auto-zero by default -- a pricing-surprise risk, but not a token/model-identity question, so out of scope for this specific bar. Rejected.
- AgentCore Memory (short-term $0.25/1,000 events; long-term storage $0.75/1,000 records/mo built-in vs $0.25/1,000 self-managed; retrieval $0.50/1,000): the built-in strategy explicitly does automatic 'summarization' before storage, which is a real token-content change on later retrieval -- but AWS never frames this as a cost-saving substitute for sending full history, only as a memory *feature*. No 'same output, cheaper' claim to test, so I did not submit it, but it is worth flagging back to the sweep as a location where a future FAIL claim could surface if a vendor markets AgentCore Memory summarization as a token-cost optimization.
- AgentCore Gateway 'Search API' / tool indexing ($0.005/1k invocations, $0.025/1k search calls, $0.02/100 tools indexed/mo): does semantic-match a subset of a large tool corpus into context per call rather than sending the full tool list -- conceptually the same shape as dedupe id 73 (mid-conversation tool changes) and id 174 (MCP cache_tools_list), so treated as already covered rather than novel; rejected to avoid restating an existing entry under a new vendor name.

Unreachable: none for this axis -- every AWS page needed was reachable via WebFetch or curl-with-UA; only one specific docs.aws.amazon.com deep link 404-redirected, and the same information was available on the pricing page instead, so no axis content was actually blocked.

axes.notes:
Checked all ten named hosts for genuine pricing/serving mechanisms (batch, dedicated/reserved capacity, caching, per-model shopping) via live curl fetches of pricing pages and docs (raw HTML for tables per rule 5, .md doc endpoints where Mintlify/docs sites exposed them). WebSearch was unavailable (session budget exhausted by other subagents), so everything below is direct fetch + grep, no secondary corroboration beyond a second independent re-fetch on the one candidate submitted.

REJECTED, considered and why:
- Groq Batch API (console.groq.com/docs/batch): flat 50% async discount, same model, standard 24h-window Batch API pattern. Grepped and confirmed live ("Batch processing lets you run thousands of API requests at scale... with 50% lower cost"), but this is the Nth instance of a pattern the register already carries at least 6 CONTRACTUAL_ONLY/FAIL entries for (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Bedrock, Azure — ids 34,63,69,77,85,137,138). Not a new mechanism, just a new vendor running the identical playbook. Dropped as non-novel.
- Together AI Batch API (docs.together.ai/docs/inference/batch/overview): confirmed "up to 50% off serverless rates," but the discount is NOT flat — only a named subset of models get 50% off; others "run at standard rates" while still batch-shaped, and dedicated-endpoint traffic gets none of it. This is a genuinely different wrinkle (discount is a separate per-model contractual choice from the async/batch mechanism itself) but it's still squarely CONTRACTUAL_ONLY/scheduling — no different tokens are read — and the underlying Batch-API pattern is already heavily represented in the dedupe file. Judged a detail on an existing entry-type, not a new one.
- Together AI 'PTUs required' dedicated-endpoint calculator, with a 'Cache hit rate %' input field: structurally identical to the Bedrock/Azure Provisioned-Throughput sizing calculators already dedup'd multiple times (ids 96,100,103,107,108,112,113,195,196). Not novel.
- Cerebras Prompt Caching (inference-docs.cerebras.ai/capabilities/prompt-caching, fetched via the site's .md endpoint): automatic, 128-token-block, 5min-1hr TTL caching with a `prompt_cache_key` routing hint explicitly documented as billing-inert ("does not affect billing"), plus a dual-bucket rate-limit rule where cached tokens count toward total TPM but not "uncached TPM." Mechanically this is the same generic prompt-caching pattern the register has already exhaustively covered across Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini/Bedrock/Azure/DeepSeek/Moonshot/StepFun/Qwen/Baidu (ids 42-45,60-64,68-69,74-77,82-85,93-98,105-107,141,147-150,163-175,184-186,199,205-207). The rate-limit dual-bucket wrinkle is structurally the same shape as the existing Anthropic ITPM exception (id 76), just generalized to all-models-with-caching instead of a Haiku-3.5-specific carve-out. Judged a minor variant, not independently novel.
- Baseten `perfCostCacheInput` fields, DeepInfra `cache_retention`/block-granularity notes, Novita `cacheReadPricing`/`cacheWrite` JSON: all just per-model instances of the same generic prompt-caching price-table pattern already covered. Not novel.
- DeepInfra Priority/Flex/Standard service tiers (confirmed via pricing page i18n strings: "Supports Priority Tier," "Supports Flex Tier," with caching rates that "scale the same way they scale input and output" across tiers): this is DeepInfra directly mirroring OpenAI's service_tier=flex/priority mechanism, terminology and all — already covered at ids 86 (FAIL) and 87 (INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE) for the OpenAI original. A copy of an already-adjudicated mechanism by a second vendor isn't a new line item.
- DeepInfra's per-model "Quantization" filter column: this is the honest version of the quantization question — DeepInfra ships quantized variants as separately-named model IDs (e.g., a "-Turbo" suffix) rather than a flag on an existing ID, so there's no spread to catch: the customer is buying an explicitly different, separately-priced product from the start, not something silently swapped under an unchanged name. Not a candidate for this register.
- Groq TruePoint Numerics (proprietary reduced-precision technology on the LPU): the only source I could locate was a 2022-dated whitepaper PDF surfaced via the Wayback Machine CDX index (groq.com/GroqDocs/GROQ ACCURACY TECH DOC - Groq TruePoint Technology.pdf); the current groq.com site returns 404 for every truepoint-numerics URL I tried (checked ~6 guessed paths plus the live sitemap.xml, which only lists 49 top-level URLs and doesn't include it). Since I could not find current, customer-facing pricing language tying TruePoint to a specific cost lever (as opposed to a general architecture description), and the one document I found is four years stale, I did not build a candidate on it. Flagging as a possible lead for a future sweep with WebSearch available, not as unreachable-but-real.
- SambaNova: cloud.sambanova.ai/pricing fetched (200, 156KB) but contains no batch, quantization, or speculative-decoding language, and only 2 generic "Cach" hits with no surrounding mechanism description — nothing to build a candidate on.
- Hyperbolic and (the sambanova.ai apex domain, as opposed to cloud.sambanova.ai) both 404'd on their pricing paths; I found the working cloud.sambanova.ai pricing URL and it yielded nothing (above), so I did not chase Hyperbolic's docs further given the marginal return already seen across this axis — noted under unreachable.
- Fireworks speculative decoding (default drafter attached automatically on most serverless deployments, confirmed live): mechanically identical to the general speculative-decoding pattern already FAIL'd twice in the dedupe file (ids 54, 55, the original Leviathan/Chen papers). A provider turning on the same already-adjudicated technique by default isn't a new mechanism.
- Replicate: pricing page fetched (86KB) but is almost entirely per-second/per-model compute pricing with essentially no batch/cache/dedicated language beyond one generic "dedicated" mention (their per-model hardware picker) — nothing distinct to report.

No repos were load-bearing for the submitted candidate (both sources are the providers' own live documentation, not GitHub projects), so rule 7's star/last-push check does not apply here.
unreachable: hyperbolic.xyz/pricing — 404 (Next.js app-router page not present at that path); did not chase further given the low yield already observed across nine of the ten providers on this axis, so no Wayback/alt-host attempt was made — flagging as a gap rather than exhausting the same low-signal search pattern a third time.

Groq TruePoint Numerics current marketing page — every guessed groq.com URL 404'd; located only a 2022 whitepaper PDF via web.archive.org's CDX index (http://web.archive.org/web/20220120200742/https://groq.com/GroqDocs/GROQ%20ACCURACY%20TECH%20DOC%20-%20Groq%20TruePoint%20Technology.pdf), too stale to found a candidate on without WebSearch (unavailable this session) to find a current source.

axes.notes:
Checked all eight named providers. Full picture:

MISTRAL — strongest coverage on this axis. docs.mistral.ai/api/ (raw HTML, 130 lines) confirmed prompt_cache_key field; docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/batch/ (raw HTML, 565 lines) confirmed 50%-discount Batch API; mistral.ai/pricing/api/ (raw HTML, 2323 lines) cross-confirmed both numbers plus surfaced a "Priority Tier" ("Priority inference for high-importance, predictable and fast compute needs") — REJECTED as a standalone candidate: no discount percentage, no contract-length/commitment terms, and no output claim anywhere near it, just a tooltip fragment. mistral.ai/pricing/enterprise-deployments/ is a contact-sales form with zero published committed-spend numbers — rejected, too thin to grade (parallel to how the register already treats bare "contact sales" claims as ungradeable without a dollar figure).

COHERE — batch job endpoints exist (docs.cohere.com/reference/create-batch, list-batches, get-batch, cancel-batch) but neither the reference pages nor the full 531KB pricing page document any batch discount — checked and rejected as a batch candidate (no percentage to cite). The cached_tokens usage field survived as candidate 3. No prompt-caching guide/concept page exists anywhere in Cohere's docs; only the bare field in the API schema.

AI21 (Jamba) — has a Batch API (docs.ai21.com/docs/jamba-batch-api) but it is "currently available for enterprise use through our SaaS offering," gated entirely behind "contact our sales team" with zero discount percentage, zero SLA, zero output-consistency language anywhere in the 39-line doc. Rejected — nothing to grade. Grepped the full 60-line llms.txt documentation index for "cach": zero hits. AI21 does not appear to offer prompt/context caching at all.

ALEPH ALPHA — now operates as PhariaAI, an enterprise sovereign-AI stack (docs.aleph-alpha.com redirects to phariaai-home). entries.name: Anthropic Compaction API (compact_20260112): AI-written summary replaces original conversation tokens on every request after it fires; the summarization pass is a separately-billed iteration excluded from top-level usage totals
entries.reasoning: Verified via raw HTML fetch of platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction (2026-08-18; not the empty-shell case, 2.5MB rendered). The docs state outright: 'The API automatically drops all content blocks prior to the compaction block, continuing the conversation from the summary' (grepped, 2 raw hits, both from one rendered paragraph duplicated once in the page's Next.js RSC hydration payload -- not two independent statements). So every request after compaction fires feeds the model an AI-generated summary in place of the real prior turns -- the provider's own stated mechanism, not a contested inference, which is sufficient for FAIL under the bar without any live measurement. Submitted quote 'Compaction requires an additional sampling step, which contributes to rate limits and billing' also confirmed in place, 2 raw hits/1 real occurrence, directly adjacent to a worked usage example showing usage.iterations containing {type:'compaction', input_tokens:180000, output_tokens:3500} that is NOT reflected in the response's top-level usage.input_tokens (23000)/usage.output_tokens (1000). The doc states this explicitly: 'The top-level input_tokens and output_tokens do not include compaction iteration usage... To calculate total tokens consumed and billed for a request, sum across all entries in the usage.iterations array' (confirmed present verbatim by byte-offset inspection; a naive single-line grep -o on raw HTML returns 0 only because the source wraps 'input_tokens'/'output_tokens' in inline <code> spans, not because the sentence is absent or spliced -- the visually-contiguous sentence is real). Not in existing-226: grepped 'compact', 'summariz', 'iteration' against all 226 entry titles, only incidental unrelated hits (entry 21's 'set iteration', entry 53's 'iteration-level scheduling').
entries.savings: Pitched as extending effective context length and keeping active context small for long-running conversations 'without client-side summarization code' -- an implicit efficiency/cost-management pitch versus manually resending an ever-growing history.
entries.provenance: Own fetch 2026-08-18, raw curl HTML (not markdown-converted), grepped directly against the source; cross-checked against existing-226.txt title list for restatement -- none found.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind billing audit -- one that reads only request/response metadata, never conversation text -- can still catch this: the response's usage.iterations array carries a {type:'compaction'} entry with real input/output token counts absent from the top-level usage.input_tokens/usage.output_tokens fields whenever compaction just fired. Any monitoring pipeline summing only the top-level fields under-reports true billed tokens for that request, visible purely from the shape of the usage object, no content required.
entries.trap: A cost dashboard that trusts usage.input_tokens/usage.output_tokens (the fields every SDK surfaces by default) silently under-counts spend the moment compaction fires, because the compaction iteration's tokens live only in usage.iterations; and on every turn after compaction, the model is reasoning over its own lossy summary of the conversation rather than the original record, so context that mattered can quietly disappear with no error or warning.
entries.settlingExperiment: Verdict rests on documentation alone (no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no live traffic this session) and needs none for FAIL -- the provider's own text establishes token non-identity structurally. A live experiment would only be needed to quantify, in dollars, the size of the top-level-usage under-count on a real long-running session, which nothing here claims to have measured.

entries.name: Gemini Live API sliding-window context eviction (contextWindowCompression) as the Live API's cost cap
entries.reasoning: Fetched ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/live-api/best-practices raw HTML (2026-08-18) and grepped the raw byte stream directly (python3 substring search, no markdown conversion). Quote 'the API automatically evicts older tokens once the threshold is reached. The API then bills subsequent turns only for the retained history plus any new tokens.' is a single contiguous sentence pair, found exactly once, sitting directly under the h3 heading 'Managing costs with context limits,' right after the doc's own description of contextWindowCompression (25,000-token trigger / 8,000-token sliding window example). quoteHits=1 confirmed, matching the candidate's claim. Control phrase 'Past tokens are re-processed and accounted for in each new turn' also found exactly once, under a separate h3 'The session context window (compounding costs).' controlHits=1 confirmed. Not present in existing-226.txt (register's Gemini caching entries — #44, #62, #93-97, #109, #169 — cover context caching, batch, and provisioned throughput, none cover Live-API turn eviction), so this is genuinely a new mechanism, not a restatement. On the bar: eviction is a documented, deliberate deletion of older turns from what the model is fed once a threshold fires. After eviction the model reads a materially smaller, different token sequence than it would without the feature — that is a structural fact about the mechanism's own definition, not something requiring a live measurement to establish. That is exactly the case the bar marks FAIL ('does the model read a different sequence of tokens... a changed product sold as a saving'), consistent with how the existing register already treats other honestly-disclosed but lossy context-trimming features (e.g. #225 context editing, #155 truncation-then-retry) as FAIL rather than exempting them for being overtly documented.
entries.savings: Uncapped otherwise, since Live API context is re-billed in full every turn as a session lengthens ('compounding costs' is Google's own term); eviction caps per-turn cost growth at the configured window size once the trigger fires. No fixed percentage — magnitude is whatever trigger/window values the developer sets.
entries.provenance: Provider documentation only (ai.google.dev), fetched and grepped directly by me on 2026-08-18; no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no live traffic, no invoice. The FAIL classification itself does not require a measurement — it follows structurally from the mechanism's own stated definition (evict = remove from what's read).
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit (token/byte counts and timing only, no message content) could observe per-turn input-token counts stop growing linearly with session length once the configured trigger threshold is crossed — but could not, from counts alone, distinguish 'the model got cheaper to run' from 'the model quietly forgot the first 20 minutes of the conversation.' Proving the latter requires a content-aware recall test, which is outside what billing telemetry can see.
entries.trap: A team that turns on sliding-window compression to cap Live API spend is trading away real memory for it: the model silently forgets any turn older than the configured window, so a long customer-support or voice session that needs to recall something said 20+ minutes earlier degrades exactly at the point the cost graph looks best — and nothing in the billing response flags that a recall failure is coming.
entries.settlingExperiment: Run matched long Live API sessions with contextWindowCompression on vs off, diff the token bill, and separately probe the model's recall accuracy on early-session facts post-eviction to quantify what the cost cap actually costs in fidelity.

entries.name: Gemini Interactions API previous_interaction_id — stateful continuation framed as a cache-hit-rate cost lever

entries.savings: Framed by Google as 'reducing token costs' via improved implicit-cache hit rate on the server-reconstructed prefix; no fixed percentage given, and Gemini's own caching docs describe implicit caching as best-effort with no hit-rate guarantee.
entries.provenance: Provider documentation only, fetched and grepped directly by me on 2026-08-18; no invoice or cache-hit measurement.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit could see the client-side request body shrink dramatically turn-over-turn (no resent history) once previous_interaction_id is adopted, but cannot tell from wire size alone whether the server-side reconstructed prompt actually hit cache or was billed as a fresh prefix — that requires inspecting the response's own usage/cache-metadata fields.
entries.trap: A team reads 'saving you from having to resend the entire chat history' and assumes the model stops re-reading it too — it doesn't; the server reconstructs and feeds the full history to the model every turn, same tokens and same thinking, so the actual savings (if any) hinges entirely on an unguaranteed cache hit. entries.settlingExperiment: Chain a real conversation via previous_interaction_id vs an equivalent full-resend conversation, and diff the usage/cache-hit fields the API returns per call to see whether the claimed cache-hit-rate improvement is real and how large it is.

entries.name: Requesty Fallback Policies marketed as 'Cost Optimization'

entries.savings: No fixed percentage; the vendor frames it as avoiding premium-model cost on every call by only escalating to a pricier model when the cheaper one errors out — but escalation is triggered by any failure, not by a cost threshold, and the app is not told when it happened.

No measurement is needed to establish that a different model can answer; that is asserted by the vendor itself.

entries.name: Eden AI Smart Routing (@edenai automatic model selection)
entries.reasoning: Setting model to '@edenai' hands per-request model selection to Eden AI's router, which on a fully successful call can answer with any of several different vendors' models (openai/gpt-4o, anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5, google/gemini-2.5-flash confirmed present together as a router_candidates example in the docs). This is proactive, not failure-triggered: two byte-identical requests can be answered by two different models from two different vendors depending on the router's cost/quality judgment. That is squarely 'a different model answers' under the bar, independent of whether the swap is disclosed in a response field. Not a duplicate of register #70 (which covers shopping across interchangeable hosts of one open-weight model's identical weights) or #211 (LiteLLM budget-triggered reroute) -- this is proactive cross-vendor closed-model substitution as the default mode of operation.
entries.savings: Not quantified by Eden AI; positioned as an automatic quality/cost balance, not a fixed discount.
entries.provenance: Eden AI's own docs page (v3/llms/smart-routing), fetched directly, not SPA-shelled -- full prerendered content present.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit could observe the model field in the request is a constant literal ('@edenai') while the model identifier that actually served each response varies across calls -- visible in response metadata/logs even without reading token content.
entries.trap: A team benchmarks or safety-tests against one vendor's model, ships with model:'@edenai', and silently drifts onto a different vendor's model (different alignment, different tool-calling quirks, different context window) on some later call with zero code change and zero visible signal in the request.
entries.settlingExperiment: Unmeasured -- no live traffic. Would require firing N identical requests through @edenai and logging which underlying model answered each one to confirm actual cross-vendor variance in practice, not just documented capability.

entries.name: Portkey Conditional Routing (business-rule model rewriting)
entries.reasoning: Portkey's Conditional Routing (confirmed available on all plans including free, via the docs' own line 'This feature is available on all Portkey plans') lets an admin's server-side Config silently rewrite an abstract request label to a concrete, different model -- the docs' own worked examples route model:'fastest' to gpt-4o-mini and model:'smartest' to openai o1, and route cost-flagged test traffic to 'the cheapest model.' Because the rule lives in the gateway Config rather than in the caller's request, an application sending the same logical target can be served by a different model whenever the admin edits the Config, with no signal in the request itself. This is 'a different model answers' by definition -- FAIL under the bar, same category as the LiteLLM Budget Fallbacks entry already in the register (#211) but a distinct vendor and a distinct triggering mechanism (arbitrary label/metadata rules vs. a specific spend-cap trigger), so not a duplicate.
entries.savings: One documented use case routes cost-flagged test traffic to 'the cheapest model'; no fixed percentage given -- magnitude depends entirely on the admin's own Config, which is exactly the point: the caller cannot know it from the request.
entries.provenance: Portkey's own docs (product/ai-gateway/conditional-routing.md), fetched as raw markdown source, not converted from HTML.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit could observe that the literal model string in the outbound request ('fastest', 'smartest', etc.) never matches the model ID that actually served the response, and that the mapping between the two can change without any change to the client's request stream.
entries.trap: A cost-conscious team sets up a Config once, is happy with the model quality at setup time, then an admin (or Portkey default behavior on a Config edit) quietly re-points 'smartest' at a cheaper model months later -- the calling code never changes and there's nothing in application logs to catch it short of inspecting the gateway Config history.
entries.settlingExperiment: Unmeasured -- no live traffic through a configured Portkey gateway to confirm the documented routing actually fires as described end to end.

entries.name: OpenRouter Free Models Router picks a random free model
entries.reasoning: model:'openrouter/free' hands selection to OpenRouter's Free Models Router, which its own cookbook states 'automatically selects a free model at random from the available free models on OpenRouter,' filtered only by feature support (tool calling, image understanding, etc). Two calls with byte-identical input can be answered by two unrelated free models purely by chance. That is unambiguously 'a different model answers' -- FAIL under the bar. Distinct from #70 (same-weights, different host) and from the register's existing OpenRouter cache-mechanics entries (#7/#65): this is explicit random model-identity selection across genuinely different free models, not present elsewhere in the register.
entries.savings: 100% of the per-call price -- the entire point of the router is $0 inference; the tradeoff is loss of control over which model answers, not a hidden cost.
entries.provenance: OpenRouter's own cookbook page, fetched as raw markdown source.

entries.name: Cerebras prompt caching carries zero cost discount — cached tokens bill at the standard input rate; only latency changes
entries.reasoning: Cerebras's own docs state plainly, confirmed verbatim: cached and freshly-computed input tokens are billed identically at the standard input rate, so a cache hit changes only time-to-first-token, never the bill. This is a documentation sentence -- the provider's word -- which per the standing rule caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY regardless of which direction the claim runs (a discount claim or, as here, an explicit no-discount claim). It does not fall to FAIL because, taken at face value, nothing about the mechanism changes what tokens the model reads, which model answers, or how much thinking happens -- caching here is a transparent compute-reuse optimization Cerebras states does not alter billing or (implicitly) output. Also confirmed: the TTL is a 5-minute guaranteed floor with a load-dependent ceiling up to 1 hour, and cached tokens count against total TPM but are excluded from the uncached TPM sub-limit -- the inverse framing of Anthropic's ITPM carve-out already in the register (id 76, which excludes cache-read tokens from the ITPM limit entirely).
entries.savings: None -- Cerebras explicitly states there is no cache-read discount; cached and uncached input tokens bill at the same standard rate. The only benefit is lower TTFT.
entries.provenance: Cerebras's own inference docs (capabilities/prompt-caching), fetched as raw HTML -- a Mintlify-style doc site with full server-rendered content, not an empty SPA shell (confirmed by grepping matched text directly in the fetched HTML, present twice: once in rendered DOM, once in the embedded page-data JSON).
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit could observe that Cerebras's invoice line items show no discounted-rate bucket for cached tokens at all -- unlike Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini, where a cache-read line item bills at a visibly lower per-token rate than a cache-miss line item, Cerebras's billing has only one input rate regardless of cache status.
entries.trap: A team migrating a caching-aware cost model from Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini to Cerebras carries over the assumption that a high cache-hit rate lowers the bill, sizes its budget accordingly, and is surprised when the invoice doesn't move -- the feature shares the name 'prompt caching' with every competitor's discount mechanism while delivering none of the discount.
entries.settlingExperiment: Unmeasured -- no live traffic and no Cerebras API key. Would require firing repeated cached vs. uncached calls against a real Cerebras account and diffing the actual invoice line items to confirm the FAQ's billing claim holds in practice, plus timing TTFT to confirm the claimed latency benefit is real.

entries.name: OpenAI GPT-5.6+ explicit cache breakpoints: 1.25x write fee, hard 30-minute TTL, and a mode that silently no-ops with zero breakpoints
entries.reasoning: Quote verified as a genuine contiguous sentence on the live page (curl of https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching, the 301 target of the platform.openai.com URL given): 'If you set mode to explicit but provide no explicit breakpoints, the request does not use prompt caching or incur cache-write charges.' entries.name: AWS Bedrock cache checkpoints: minimum quadruples on newest Claude models (1,024 → 4,096), and misses fail open silently
entries.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim via curl of https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html: 'Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 require at least 4,096 tokens per cache checkpoint' — 1 exact hit, part of one unbroken sentence, and independently confirmed in the page's own supported-models table. The silent fail-open claim is also directly stated on the page: 'If you try to add a cache checkpoint before meeting the minimum number of tokens, your inference will still succeed, but your prefix will not be cached.' One accuracy caveat worth flagging: the candidate's headline framing ('minimum quadruples on newest Claude models') slightly overstates the pattern — the same table lists Claude Sonnet 4.6 at a 1,024-token minimum, so it is not strictly true that every newer-generation model needs more tokens; the specific four models named in the quote are correctly described, but 'newest = higher minimum' does not hold universally. Checked against existing-226.txt: entry 26 covers this same shape of claim (Haiku needing a longer prefix than Sonnet/Opus) but is scoped to Anthropic's direct API per the candidate's novelty note; entry 27 covers only the cache_control<->cachePoint dialect translation; entry 98 is a generic, undetailed 'AWS Bedrock prompt caching' line. entries.savings: Reduced per-token rate on cache reads when the model-specific minimum is met; zero savings, silently, whenever the prefix falls under that model's minimum — with no error surfaced.
entries.provenance: curl -sL of the cited AWS doc URL (59KB raw HTML), tags stripped, grep for the exact quoted sentence: 1 hit. Control phrase 'cache checkpoint' independently counted at 35 exact-case hits (candidate claimed 29 — both strongly non-zero, confirming the fetch is real and not a broken/empty page; the discrepancy is not investigated further since the check's only purpose is ruling out a broken fetch). Documentation-only; no measurement performed.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit CAN observe this from usage metadata alone: cacheReadInputTokens/cacheWriteInputTokens in the Converse API response would show a system prompt that previously produced nonzero cache reads on an older same-family model suddenly reading 0 after a same-length prefix is sent to a newer model requiring 4,096 tokens — visible from token-count fields, no prompt content needed.

entries.name: Fireworks AI prompt caching: no fixed TTL (minutes to hours, load-dependent, LRU eviction), and a shared cache with a self-disclosed timing-attack risk
entries.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim via curl of https://docs.fireworks.ai/guides/prompt-caching: 'usually stay in the cache for at least several minutes' — found as part of one unbroken sentence ('Cached prompts usually stay in the cache for at least several minutes. Depending on the model, load level, and deployment configuration, it can be up to several hours.'), 2 hits (again the doc site duplicates content once as rendered prose and once as an escaped JSX string literal — confirmed by inspecting both matches directly, they are the same sentence). Also independently confirmed on-page: 'The oldest prompts are evicted from the cache first' (LRU); 'Dedicated deployments by default share a single cache across all requests'; 'It does open a minor risk of a timing attack: potentially, an adversary can learn that a particular prompt is cached by observing the response time'; and the opt-in mitigation via the x-prompt-cache-isolation-key header / prompt_cache_isolation_key field. Notably the same page also states 'Prompt caching doesn't alter the result generated by the model' — the provider's own no-content-change assertion, which is exactly the kind of claim that caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY rather than PASS_ABSOLUTE absent measurement. Checked against existing-226.txt: Fireworks AI does not appear anywhere in the register. No fixed TTL, LRU eviction, and the self-disclosed cross-tenant timing side-channel are new facts for a new provider. Documentation only, no Fireworks API key or live/co-tenant access available in this environment, so caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY as proposed.
entries.savings: Default 50% discount (model-dependent) on cached serverless tokens; near-free reuse on dedicated deployments since cached tokens skip reprocessing — but with no committed floor on how long that reuse window lasts.

entries.settlingExperiment: The timing-attack risk cannot be confirmed content-blind or from documentation alone — it would require provisioning two co-tenant accounts on the same shared dedicated deployment, sending a distinctive prompt from tenant A, then measuring tenant B's response latency for the identical prompt to see if it drops (indicating a cache hit leaked across tenants). Not attempted here; no dedicated-deployment access or second tenant account available in this environment.
entries.telemetrySignal: Mostly NOT observable content-blind: the variable TTL (minutes to hours, load-dependent) and LRU eviction are internal scheduling behavior with no exposed metadata field to watch. The cross-tenant timing-attack risk is explicitly a side-channel that requires an active timing measurement across two accounts, not passive request/response metadata — a content-blind audit of one tenant's own traffic cannot detect it at all.

entries.name: xAI Grok prompt caching: reasoning_content replay requirement is the documented top cause of silent cache misses; no TTL guarantee at all
entries.reasoning: Verified against the live page at the second attempt (first curl returned a soft-404 'Models | SpaceXAI Docs' shell with 0 hits for every search term — a transient routing glitch, not evidence the page is fake; a clean refetch returned the real page titled 'What Breaks Caching | SpaceXAI Docs'). On the real page, the candidate's quote 'omitting it is the top cause of cache misses' is a genuine contiguous substring — I get 1 hit (candidate claimed 2; the true count is 1), sitting at the end of the sentence '...must include reasoning_content from previous responses; omitting it is the top cause of cache misses.' Control phrase 'x-grok-conv-id' hits 18 times on that page (candidate claimed 10; true count is 18 — still nonzero and clearly present, so the control isn't a false negative, just miscounted by the submitter). Quote is real and correctly attributed. HOWEVER: the mechanism paragraph also wraps a second string in quote marks — 'can be evicted at any time due to server load or restarts' — that does NOT appear verbatim anywhere in xAI's caching docs. I checked all five caching subpages (overview, how-it-works, best-practices, maximizing-cache-hits, usage-and-pricing) plus multi-turn: the real eviction language is 'Cache entries can be evicted due to memory pressure, and requests may be routed to different servers' (how-it-works) and 'Eviction and routing mean cache hits aren't guaranteed' (best-practices) — no mention of 'server load' or 'restarts' anywhere. That phrase is a fabricated/paraphrased quote dressed as verbatim inside the mechanism narrative (not in the formal 'quote' field, but still the exact defect Hard Rule 3/4 warns about) and should be struck or rewritten as plain paraphrase before this entry is filed. The 'no TTL floor or ceiling at all' claim is accurate as an absence-of-evidence observation — I found zero occurrences of 'TTL' across all six caching pages, consistent with xAI never publishing a TTL number. Applying the bar: this is entirely documentation describing xAI's own cache-invalidation trigger and pricing discount, with zero independent measurement possible (no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no xAI key, no live traffic) — provider's word caps it at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. Cache hit vs. miss is not a FAIL under the bar either way, since both paths are documented to produce the same output tokens — only the compute-reuse and price differ.
entries.savings: Cached prompt tokens billed at a reduced 'cached prompt token price' per xAI's pricing page — confirmed the discount exists in principle via the cache-hit/cache-miss framing on the docs, but the exact percentage is not stated on the caching pages themselves and was not independently priced in this sweep.
entries.provenance: curl-fetched https://docs.x.ai/developers/advanced-api-usage/prompt-caching/multi-turn twice (first attempt soft-404'd, second attempt succeeded, title 'What Breaks Caching | SpaceXAI Docs'); extracted the Next.js RSC payload from self.__next_f.push(...) chunks and grepped the decoded text directly, 2026-08-18.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit can observe whether the client resends a reasoning_content field/value on turn 2+ (field-presence check on the request body, no message content needed) and can read xAI's usage object for a cached-vs-total token split to see hit/miss. It cannot observe the internal cause of any given eviction (memory pressure vs. rerouting vs. anything else) — that is only visible in xAI's own infra logs, never in anything the customer's machine sees.
entries.trap: A harness that strips 'internal-looking' fields before persisting conversation history (a common sanitization step) silently discards reasoning_content and gets a 100% cache miss on every follow-up turn with no error — full price is charged and nothing in the response flags why the expected discount never showed up. Separately, because no TTL is published, any cost model that assumes a cache survives a fixed window (the way Anthropic's 5m/1h TTLs allow) will be wrong in either direction — the cache can vanish sooner or persist longer than assumed.
entries.settlingExperiment: Send two structurally identical multi-turn conversations to a Grok reasoning model under the same x-grok-conv-id: one that echoes reasoning_content back on turn 2, one that sends only the visible assistant text. Compare the cached-token count in each turn-2 usage object to confirm the omission produces a measurable, reproducible miss (not just a documented one).

entries.name: DeepSeek off-peak time-of-day pricing (synchronous API, not a batch job)
entries.reasoning: Fully verified on DeepSeek's Docusaurus-rendered (server-side, non-JS-gated) Models & Pricing page. Grepped the exact quote 'Off-peak rates are half of the peak rates. Peak hours are 01:00 - 04:00 and 06:00 - 10:00 UTC (all other hours are off-peak).' — 1 hit, exact match, candidate's count was correct. Control phrase 'The expense = number of tokens × price.' — 1 hit, exact match, correct. The full page content (read in full, not just grepped) confirms the mechanism: a single pricing table for the ordinary chat endpoint (base URL https://api.deepseek.com, models DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 / DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813) shows OFF-PEAK and PEAK rows for cache-hit input, cache-miss input, and output tokens — there is no batch/async/JSONL language anywhere on this page, confirming this is genuinely the synchronous path, not a relabeled batch tier. Applying the bar directly: same tokens, same model, same amount of thinking — the only variable that changes the price is the wall-clock UTC hour the request lands in. That is the textbook case the PASS_SCHEDULING category exists for, and unlike the register's existing batch-discount entries (which restructure the request into an async job with a different submission/polling shape and are rightly capped CONTRACTUAL_ONLY), nothing about the request pipeline itself changes here. One correction to the candidate's own arithmetic: peak hours are 01:00-04:00 (3 hours) + 06:00-10:00 (4 hours) = 7 hours/day, so off-peak is 17 of 24 hours, not the 'roughly 20' the candidate's savings field states — I've corrected this below.
entries.savings: 50% off cache-hit input, cache-miss input, and output tokens for 17 of every 24 hours (all hours except 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC) — corrected from the candidate's 'roughly 20 hours,' which overstates the off-peak window by about 3 hours/day.
entries.provenance: curl-fetched https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing, 2026-08-18; page is server-rendered (Docusaurus), full pricing table and footnotes present in the raw HTML with no JS-only gating, tag-stripped and grepped directly.
entries.telemetrySignal: Trivially observable by a content-blind audit: compare the request's UTC timestamp against the published peak/off-peak windows and the per-token rate on the resulting invoice line — pure metadata, no message content needed at all.
entries.trap: This is a genuine no-code-change saving, but it's UTC-gated, not local-time-gated — a US-based team scheduling batch/cron jobs for 'off-hours, our time' can easily land inside DeepSeek's 06:00-10:00 UTC peak window (11pm-3am US Pacific) and pay double while believing they've optimized for off-peak.
entries.settlingExperiment: Fire the byte-identical request body to the synchronous endpoint at two timestamps, one inside 06:00-10:00 UTC and one outside it, and diff the per-token billed rate in each response's usage/invoice object to confirm only price changes and token counts/content are unaffected.

The bar states explicitly: 'A documentation sentence is THE PROVIDER'S WORD, however plainly it reads, and caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY... Only a measurement, or a structural argument that no request was ever sent, supports PASS_ABSOLUTE.' This candidate supplies neither — the 'no redeploy, no model swap' claim is paraphrased directly from Microsoft's own assurance about its internal billing architecture, not an independently verifiable protocol fact (unlike, e.g., a field's presence in an HTTP header vs. the request body). Correct verdict is CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, matching the rest of the Azure PTU Reservation family already logged (id103, id107, id112, id195 — all CONTRACTUAL_ONLY). The entry is legitimately incremental — its specific quoted sentence and the cross-deployment-type exchange detail aren't verbatim in those prior entries' descriptions — so it survives the dedupe check, but not at the tier requested.

entries.name: Oban Unique Jobs — default :successful state-scope silently substitutes a stale completed job for a requested re-run
entries.reasoning: Oban is a self-hosted Elixir job-processing library, not a third-party API — the dedup decision runs inside the customer's own process against their own Postgres DB. Oban.insert/2's :unique option defaults to the state group :successful, documented verbatim as 'Jobs that aren't cancelled or discarded (default)' — confirmed on hexdocs to include the terminal :completed state, not just in-flight states. Combined with :period, whose type spec on the same page is literally `unique_period() :: Oban.Period.t() | :infinity`, a caller who calls Oban.insert/2 a second time with byte-identical args/queue/worker gets silently handed back a reference to an OLD, already-executed job — no new job row, no new execution. If that job's body calls an LLM, the second call the developer explicitly asked for never happens: zero thinking occurs where a fresh run was expected. That is 'a different amount of thinking happens' under the bar as written. Same failure family as the register's existing Sidekiq Enterprise Unique Jobs entry (216, FAIL) — a self-hosted queue whose default lock/unique key is content-derived, but whose default STATE SCOPE silently overreaches into work that already finished, not just work still in flight.
entries.savings: Marketed as 'Duplicate work can be avoided through unique job controls' (Oban.html feature list, quote confirmed verbatim, 1 hit). In practice, with default states and a long/infinite period, it can replace a fresh worker execution — and any LLM call inside it — with a reference to an arbitrarily old completed job, indistinguishable from a real new run unless the caller diffs job.id/inserted_at themselves.
entries.provenance: https://hexdocs.pm/oban/Oban.Job.html — quote 'Jobs that aren't cancelled or discarded (default)' grep-verified 1/1 hit (both python str.count and rg -o agree); control phrase 'Construct a new job changeset ready for insertion into the database' 2/2 hits, confirms fetch integrity. Same page's type spec directly shows `unique_period() :: Oban.Period.t() | :infinity` (1 hit for 'infinity' on the page), confirming the :period: :infinity claim — this required a second, more careful grep pass after an initial context-window search missed it. Marketing quote 'Duplicate work can be avoided through unique job controls' confirmed 1/1 hit on https://hexdocs.pm/oban/Oban.html. NOTE: the candidate's claim that the default dedup-key fields are 'job args + queue + worker' was NOT independently re-confirmed on the cited page in this pass (not found via search) — flagged as an assumption carried from general Oban familiarity, not from a grepped citation on the cited URL, though it does not affect the FAIL-supporting core claim (state scope + period).
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit watching only outbound LLM API traffic would see call volume undercount vs. Oban.insert/2 call volume — N inserts, fewer than N outbound model calls — with no per-call marker distinguishing genuinely new work from a unique-collision return of an old job. Oban emits telemetry events (e.g. [:oban, :job, :stop]) only for jobs that actually execute, so a skipped duplicate produces no telemetry event at all, not even a labeled skip.
providers: Oban / Oban Labs (Elixir job-processing library — hexdocs.pm/oban, oban.pro)
entries.trap: Anyone using unique: [period: :infinity] (or any long period) with the default :successful state scope on a job whose body makes a paid LLM call, expecting 'unique' to just prevent accidental double-clicks, will find that an intentional, legitimate reprocessing request (same args, different real-world moment) is silently absorbed into the ancient completed job — no error, no new row, no new model call.
entries.settlingExperiment: Not measured (no live Oban/Postgres instance, no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, in this environment). Would settle by: run Oban locally, Oban.insert a job with unique: [period: :infinity] wrapping a fake call_llm worker, let it complete, then Oban.insert an identical job again and assert (a) no new row appears in the oban_jobs table and (b) the worker's perform/1 is never invoked a second time.

entries.name: Dagster sensor run_key — content-blind key silently drops runs whose run_config differs
entries.reasoning: Dagster sensors run inside the customer's own deployment (OSS core, also sold as Dagster+ cloud). The docs state directly: 'Dagster will skip processing requests with previously used run keys, ensuring that duplicate runs won't be created' — an unambiguous statement that the skip check is keyed on run_key ALONE, not on the accompanying run_config. The docs' own basic-sensor example sets run_key=filename, confirming the key is typically a narrow, developer-chosen slice of the trigger, not a hash of the full RunRequest. Because run_key and run_config are independent parameters, two RunRequests can share a run_key while differing in run_config (different prompt/parameters passed into a downstream op), and Dagster's documented behavior launches only the first — the second is silently skipped, no run, no error. If a downstream op calls an LLM, that second, distinct call never happens: zero thinking where fresh thinking was requested. Same 'caller-supplied, content-blind key -> zero execution on collision' pattern as the register's existing BullMQ (189, FAIL) and Sidekiq (216, FAIL) entries, on a structurally distinct orchestrator not previously logged.
entries.savings: Marketed as 'preventing duplicate runs.' Actual documented behavior: any two RunRequests sharing a run_key produce exactly one run, even when their run_config differs — the second call's distinct content is never executed, silently.
entries.provenance: https://docs.dagster.io/guides/automate/sensors — primary quote 'To prevent duplicate runs, you can use run keys to uniquely identify each' grep-verified 1/1 hit (contiguous substring confirmed with grep -o). Control phrase 'Cursors and high volume events' — CORRECTED count is 4 hits, not the candidate's reported 2 (still nonzero, confirms fetch integrity; the discrepancy is in the reported number, not a fetch problem). Independently pulled and verified a second, cleaner supporting quote: 'Dagster will skip processing requests with previously used run keys, ensuring that duplicate runs won't be created' (1/1 hit) plus run_key=filename verbatim in the fetched basic-sensor code block. FLAG: the candidate's OTHER supporting quote — rendered as 'new runs won't be launched... This is because the run keys associated with the files won't change' — is a splice I do not rely on. The real admonition on the page is typed 'note' (class admonition-note), not 'caution' as the candidate wrote, and its actual literal conditional is 'if the cursor is reset but the files don't change,' a cursor-reset scenario, not the 'run_config changes but run_key doesn't' framing the candidate attributed to it. I verified this directly by reading the surrounding admonition HTML. This verdict rests only on the two clean, non-spliced quotes above, which independently establish the same core FAIL mechanism without needing that note.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit watching Dagster's run-launch events (DagsterInstance Run records) would see a RunRequest yielded by the sensor's evaluate_tick that never materializes into a Run row when its run_key collides — the sensor tick reports skipped run keys in its own tick history, so the skip is visible inside Dagster, but nothing on the LLM-provider side would show any anomaly since no request was ever made.
entries.trap: A developer who names run_key by a stable identifier (a filename, a source-record ID), believing 'duplicate' only means the exact same trigger event fired twice, will find that a second, materially different run_config sharing that same identifier is dropped just as silently as a true duplicate — no run, no error, and per the docs' own note, no easy fix except never setting run_key at all if the cursor might reset.
entries.settlingExperiment: Not measured (no live Dagster deployment here). Would settle by: define a sensor yielding two RunRequests with the same run_key but different run_config (differing an op input consumed by a fake LLM-calling op), run the sensor tick, and assert only one Run is created and the op body executed exactly once.

entries.name: Trigger.dev idempotencyKey — narrow caller-supplied key, collision returns the first run's handle instead of executing the second trigger
entries.reasoning: Trigger.dev is a managed third-party task-execution API — the trigger call does leave the customer's machine and reach Trigger.dev's servers, so this is not a 'no request ever sent' situation. Documentation states idempotency is enforced 'at the task level' via a caller-supplied idempotencyKey, and on a second trigger sharing that key, the second request does not create a new task run — instead the original run's handle is returned (verified phrasing in provenance). This is a direct, explicit statement that the SECOND request's task body — and any LLM call inside it — is never executed; the caller gets back a reference to the FIRST run's result instead. Because idempotencyKeys.create() lets the developer hash an arbitrary subset of fields (only the run ID is auto-injected when called inside a task; the full payload is not automatically folded in), two triggers with genuinely different task input can collide on a reused/narrow key, and the second's distinct content is silently discarded — zero execution for content the caller explicitly submitted. Same family as the register's existing Sidekiq/BullMQ FAILs, on a separately-documented SaaS provider not previously logged.
entries.savings: Positioned as preventing duplicate child-task creation on parent-task retries. As documented, it dedupes on the key alone — a distinctly different second request reusing a key is dropped and gets back the first run's stale handle instead of running.
entries.provenance: https://trigger.dev/docs/idempotency. CORRECTION TO THE CANDIDATE'S QUOTE: the full sentence as submitted is not a literally contiguous substring of the raw fetched page — Trigger.dev's docs ship as compiled Next.js/MDX JSX source in which the word 'idempotencyKey' sits inside a separate _jsx(_components.code,...) call, splitting the sentence around that one inline-code span. Confirmed identically on a direct curl fetch AND an independent Wayback Machine snapshot (timestamp 20260420170911) — ruling out a transient CDN/build artifact; both show the same split. I cross-checked with WebFetch (a second, independent render/instrument), which returned the identical sentence verbatim, confirming the wording is genuine and not fabricated. I then isolated a SHORTER string that IS a literal contiguous substring of the raw source on both the curl fetch and the Wayback snapshot: 'the second request will not create a new task run. Instead, the original run's handle is returned, allowing you to track the existing run's progress.' (curly right-single-quote apostrophes as in source) — verified 3/3 hits via exact python substring count. Per the grading rule (quote a shorter contiguous string if the full one isn't contiguous), I am relying on this shorter quote, not the candidate's longer one. Control phrase 'Why use idempotency keys?' — corrected count is 5 hits (python), confirms fetch integrity.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit watching Trigger.dev's own dashboard/API would see the second trigger() call return HTTP 200 with a run handle, indistinguishable at the API-response-shape level from a freshly created run unless the caller explicitly checks whether the returned run id matches one they've already seen; the quoted documentation describes no separate 'this was deduped' flag.
entries.trap: A team that reuses idempotencyKeys across retries of a parent task, believing the guard only catches literal retries, will find that any second call sharing that key — even one carrying a genuinely different payload — silently returns the FIRST run's handle, with the second payload's content never touching the task body at all.
entries.settlingExperiment: Not measured (no Trigger.dev account/API key in this environment). Would settle by: trigger a task twice with the same idempotencyKey but different payloads, and confirm from the run dashboard that only one run (with the FIRST payload) ever executed, and the second call's payload appears nowhere in the executed run's logs.

entries.name: Hatchet idempotency key_expression — narrow CEL slice of input, event-triggered collisions silently swallowed with no run and no error
entries.reasoning: Hatchet is a durable-execution/task-orchestration platform (self-hostable OSS plus Hatchet Cloud) whose idempotency is configured by a developer-written CEL key_expression evaluated over task input — confirmed on the cited page's own worked examples, which use key_expression="input.id" (27 occurrences of the literal string 'input.id' across the fetched page's examples), not a hash of the full input. The docs state plainly, for event-triggered tasks specifically: the idempotency collision 'will be swallowed, and no additional runs will be created, but the event will still be ingested correctly without an error being raised.' That is an explicit, first-party statement that the event genuinely reaches Hatchet (it is 'ingested correctly') but the task run — and anything the task body would do, including an LLM call — silently never executes on a key collision, with zero surfaced error. Since key_expression is scoped to whatever field(s) the developer names, two events sharing that field but differing elsewhere in payload collide, and the second event's distinct content produces no execution at all — a different amount of thinking (zero) than the caller's second, genuinely distinct event warranted.
entries.savings: Sold as preventing 'more than one run of a task from occurring within a given time window' (e.g. duplicate webhook sends). As documented, collisions on the narrow key expression are silently swallowed with no error and no new run, regardless of what else differs in the input.
entries.provenance: https://docs.hatchet.run/v1/idempotency — quote 'In other cases, such as triggering by events, the idempotency collision will be swallowed, and no additional runs will be created' grep-verified 2/2 hits (the page embeds both a rendered-HTML copy and a JSON/RSC-serialized copy of the same paragraph — both literal and mutually consistent, unlike the Trigger.dev page which split around inline code). Control phrase 'TTL-based idempotency requires two parameters' 2/2 hits, confirms fetch integrity. Independently confirmed key_expression="input.id" and the fallback_ttl variant verbatim in the fetched examples.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit of Hatchet's own event stream would see the event accepted (ingested, acknowledged) with no corresponding task run created and no error event emitted — per the docs' own wording the swallow is deliberately silent and error-free, so nothing downstream (logs, webhooks, dead-letter queues) would flag it.
entries.trap: A team using an event-triggered Hatchet task keyed on e.g. input.id, expecting idempotency to guard only against literal event re-delivery (webhook retries), will find that two DISTINCT events sharing that one field collide — the second event is accepted by Hatchet's ingestion layer (producers see success) but its task body, and any LLM call inside it, never runs, with no error anywhere signaling the loss.
entries.settlingExperiment: Not measured (no Hatchet instance/API key here). Would settle by: register an event-triggered task with key_expression="input.id" and a fake LLM-calling step, fire two events with the same input.id but different other payload fields, and confirm only one task run (and one simulated LLM call) occurs while the second event still returns success at ingestion.

entries.name: Envoy AI Gateway Header and Body Mutations rewrites JSON request-body fields (temperature, max_tokens, service_tier, arbitrary top-level keys) in transit
entries.reasoning: Mechanism confirmed directly from the docs page (Docusaurus SSG — full content present in the raw server-rendered HTML, not a JS-only shell). Re-grepped the candidate's quote against the raw HTML and got 3 hits, not the 1 the candidate reported (candidate under-counted but the quote is real, contiguous, and not spliced — no discrepancy in substance, just in the reported count). The 'Setting Body Fields' section shows a bodyMutation.set example setting service_tier, max_tokens, and temperature together, and Example 2 (AIGatewayRoute) bumps max_tokens for a matched gpt-4 route. Docs explicitly state nested field paths are NOT available, confirming the candidate's 'top-level keys' framing. This is a real, admin-configured, transparent-to-client capability that rewrites decoding/generation parameters (temperature changes the sampling distribution, max_tokens caps/truncates output length, service_tier changes processing tier) between the client and the model backend, on every matching request, with nothing in the response or client-visible protocol signaling that a rewrite occurred. That is squarely 'the model reads different tokens / a different amount of thinking happens' under the bar — temperature and max_tokens are inputs the model's sampler directly consumes. It is not marketed as a savings feature by name (savings field correctly says so), but the register's bar is about mechanism, not marketing copy, and this is a documented, shipped, generally-available capability (repo envoyproxy/ai-gateway: 1,937 stars, not archived, pushed within the last day — actively maintained, load-bearing and real) rather than a hypothetical. Verdict: FAIL.
entries.savings: Not sold as a savings feature by name — documented as a generic ops capability (add org headers, strip internal fields, set service tiers per route/backend). But the shipped worked examples use it to alter service_tier, max_tokens, and temperature, and nothing prevents an operator from using it to silently cap max_tokens or force a cheaper service_tier for cost control with zero client-visible signal.
entries.provenance: Raw HTML fetch of https://aigateway.envoyproxy.io/docs/capabilities/traffic/header-body-mutations (Docusaurus v3.10.1, content present server-side). Quote 'Envoy AI Gateway allows you to mutate HTTP headers and JSON request body fields before requests are sent to backends.' greps 3x in raw HTML. Control phrase 'Header and Body Mutations' greps 7x (candidate reported 5x) — both present and not zero, ruling out a broken-fetch false negative. Verified bodyMutation/headerMutation/service_tier/max_tokens/temperature keywords all present in the doc's YAML examples. Repo envoyproxy/ai-gateway confirmed live via `gh api`: 1,937 stars, not archived, last push 2026-08-18.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit (one that inspects only client-observed request/response bytes, timing, or billing totals) cannot detect this at all — the mutation happens inside the gateway's data plane, between the gateway and the model backend, strictly downstream of anything the client or a client-side logging layer can see. Detecting it requires operator-side config review or a diff between client-sent bytes and backend-received bytes captured at the gateway.
entries.trap: An operator (or a compromised/misconfigured gateway config) can quietly cap max_tokens, drop temperature, or downgrade service_tier for cost control on a route the client believes is unmodified — the client has no protocol-level way to detect that its request was rewritten before the model saw it.

entries.name: AWS Bedrock Runtime: boto3/botocore (legacy retry mode) and aws-sdk-go-v2 both retry client-side read-timeout by default on non-idempotent InvokeModel/Converse calls
entries.reasoning: Fully source-verified, not doc-derived. (1) botocore/retryhandler.py: EXCEPTION_MAP['GENERAL_CONNECTION_ERROR'] includes ReadTimeoutError — quote greps exactly 1x, verbatim, contiguous (lines 33-40). (2) botocore/data/_retry.json: '__default__' policy sets max_attempts: 5 and includes general_socket_errors (line 93, 100). (3) botocore/client.py line 320: `return config_store.get_config_variable('retry_mode') or 'legacy'` — confirms the legacy-by-default claim verbatim. (4) botocore/data/bedrock-runtime/.../service-2.json: parsed with Python's json module — InvokeModelRequest members are ['body','contentType','accept','modelId','trace','guardrailIdentifier','guardrailVersion','performanceConfigLatency','serviceTier','requestMetadata'] and ConverseRequest members similarly carry no token field; StartAsyncInvokeRequest DOES carry 'clientRequestToken', shape AsyncInvokeIdempotencyToken with idempotencyToken:true (line 4489) — confirming the real-time path has no idempotency mechanism while the async batch path does.
