(6) aws-sdk-go-v2/aws/retry/retryable_error.go lines 79-84: RetryableConnectionError's doc comment 'Includes errors such as connection reset, connection refused, net dial, temporary, and timeout errors' matches the candidate's citation verbatim. Every specific, checkable claim in this candidate checked out against the actual source of two independently-implemented official AWS SDKs. This is a structural (source-code-grounded) finding, not a vendor-documentation assertion, and it describes a real mechanism by which the model reads the identical prompt a second time and produces a second, separately billed generation — squarely the bar's FAIL condition.
entries.savings: None — this is a waste finding, not a savings claim, as the candidate itself states. Confirmed defaults: legacy retry_mode, max_attempts=5 (botocore); DefaultMaxAttempts=3 (aws-sdk-go-v2); no idempotency token on the real-time inference input shapes in either SDK's service model.
entries.provenance: Fetched and grepped directly: raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/{botocore/retryhandler.py, botocore/client.py, botocore/data/_retry.json, botocore/data/bedrock-runtime/2023-09-30/service-2.json} and raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/main/aws/retry/{standard.go, retryable_error.go}. service-2.json parsed with Python's json module to enumerate InvokeModelRequest/ConverseRequest/StartAsyncInvokeRequest member lists directly rather than trusting a text search. Repos verified live via `gh api`: boto/botocore 1,637 stars pushed 2026-08-18, aws/aws-sdk-go-v2 3,628 stars pushed 2026-08-18, neither archived.
entries.settlingExperiment: This one specific piece would benefit from a live measurement: fire an InvokeModel call against a real Bedrock endpoint with a client read-timeout set shorter than a typical generation, and check AWS Cost Explorer / CloudWatch usage metrics for two billed invocations with identical request-body hashes in the same time window. No ANTHROPIC/AWS credentials are available in this sweep, so that measurement was not performed — the FAIL verdict here rests on the code-level mechanism (retry-with-no-idempotency-token is real and default-on), not on an observed double bill.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind billing-log audit COULD catch this in principle — two InvokeModel/Converse line items with identical request-body hashes and close timestamps following a client-side read-timeout — but nothing in Bedrock's response metadata flags the second call as a retry-of-the-first, so the audit has to correlate by body hash and timing itself; there is no first-class 'this was a retry' signal exposed anywhere in the API.
entries.trap: Anyone running default-configured botocore or aws-sdk-go-v2 against Bedrock Runtime for long-generation or slow-model InvokeModel/Converse calls is one client read-timeout away from being silently billed for the same generation twice (up to 5x under legacy botocore), with no idempotency key available anywhere in the request shape to prevent or even detect it after the fact.

entries.name: google-genai (Gemini/Vertex AI) Python SDK ships with retries fully OFF by default -- the one major SDK studied where the default eliminates the retry-inflicted double-billing surface entirely
entries.reasoning: Fully source-verified, not doc-derived. google/genai/_api_client.py lines 572-573 grep exactly 1x, verbatim, matching the candidate's quote precisely (2-space indentation and all): `if options is None: return {'stop': tenacity.stop_after_attempt(1), 'reraise': True}`. Control phrase 'def retry_args(options: Optional[HttpRetryOptions])' also verified at 1 hit (line 562). google/genai/types.py line 2665: `retry_options: Optional[HttpRetryOptions] = Field(default=None, ...)` confirmed. google/genai/_api_client.py line 719: BaseApiClient.__init__ unconditionally executes `self._http_options = HttpOptions()` before any user override is merged in (lines 691-719 show validated_http_options only overrides when the caller explicitly passes http_options as a dict or duck-typed object) — so a zero-config client genuinely resolves to retry_options=None and therefore retry_args(None), i.e. exactly one attempt, reraise, no retry loop entered at all. Also cross-checked the opt-in defaults candidate cited: _RETRY_ATTEMPTS=5, _RETRY_INITIAL_DELAY=1.0, _RETRY_HTTP_STATUS_CODES=(408,429,500,502,503,504) all verified verbatim at lines 547-559. This is the strongest evidence category available without a live measurement: inspected source code (not vendor documentation prose) directly showing that on the default code path, a failure is reraised to the caller after exactly one attempt — a structural argument that no duplicate request is ever sent by the SDK itself. Independently reconfirmed the candidate's contrast claim for anthropic-sdk-python's _constants.py: DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES = 2, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = httpx.Timeout(timeout=10*60, connect=5.0) — both match exactly, lines 9-10.
entries.savings: Avoids the retry-double-billing surface entirely by default (no request is ever silently resent unless a developer explicitly opts in via HttpRetryOptions). This is a savings-by-absence-of-waste finding, source-verified rather than asserted by Google's documentation.
entries.provenance: Fetched and grepped directly: raw.githubusercontent.com/googleapis/python-genai/main/google/genai/{_api_client.py, types.py, client.py} and raw.githubusercontent.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/main/src/anthropic/_constants.py. entries.telemetrySignal: Cannot be observed by a content-blind audit — this is an absence (no retry fires), not a signal that appears on the wire. Confirming it requires either reading the client library source (as done here) or deliberately forcing a timeout/5xx against a live endpoint and observing that no automatic second request follows; a request/response-log audit alone cannot distinguish 'retry disabled' from 'retry enabled but not triggered this time.'
entries.trap: Not a trap for users of this SDK as shipped — the trap is for anyone who assumes google-genai behaves like the Anthropic/OpenAI SDKs (which retry automatically by default) and wraps it in their own blind outer retry loop 'to be safe,' which reintroduces exactly the duplicate-billing risk this SDK's default was designed to avoid.

entries.name: Azure AI Inference SDK's default RetryPolicy will not retry a POST after a client-side timeout, only after an explicit 5xx response — exception-vs-status-code paths use different rules
entries.reasoning: Verified directly against source, not docs. On Azure/azure-sdk-for-python@main (2026-08-18): azure-core's RetryPolicyBase.__init__ sets self._method_whitelist = frozenset(["HEAD","GET","PUT","DELETE","OPTIONS","TRACE"]) — POST/PATCH absent (2 hits for '_method_whitelist', matching claim: the definition at line 94 and the 'methods' default lookup at line 122). azure-ai-inference's _configuration.py builds self.retry_policy = kwargs.get('retry_policy') or policies.RetryPolicy(**kwargs) at all 3 client-construction call sites, confirming azure-ai-inference uses this policy by default. _is_method_retryable()'s POST/PATCH+5xx carve-out at line 203 only fires 'if response and ...'; on the exception path (line 558, 'except AzureError as err: ... self._is_method_retryable(retry_settings, request.http_request)') no response kwarg is passed, so it's None/falsy, the carve-out never executes, and POST falls through to 'not in settings["methods"]' → returns False → raise err with zero retry request constructed or sent. This is a structural, code-level proof that a client-side read/connect timeout on a POST puts exactly one request on the wire, never two — exactly the 'structural argument that no request was ever sent' the bar requires for PASS_ABSOLUTE. Cross-checked openai-python's src/openai/_constants.py: DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES = 2, no method-based gating there, confirming the candidate's differentiation claim (AzureOpenAI via the openai package does NOT get this protection; only azure-core-based clients do) is accurate.
entries.savings: Avoids a timeout-retry double-request (and thus double-generation-billing) vector by default, specifically for POST calls through azure-ai-inference / any azure-core-based Azure AI SDK, on the client-side-timeout failure path only. Does not apply to Azure OpenAI accessed via openai-python's AzureOpenAI class (bypasses azure-core; inherits openai's own DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES=2 with no method restriction — confirmed in source). Does not apply to a POST that gets back an explicit 500/503/504 status — that IS retried by default via the separate carve-out.
entries.provenance: curl'd raw GitHub source directly (not WebFetch/markdown): sdk/core/azure-core/azure/core/pipeline/policies/_retry.py (576 lines) and sdk/ai/azure-ai-inference/azure/ai/inference/_configuration.py (188 lines), Azure/azure-sdk-for-python@main, fetched 2026-08-18. A confirmatory (non-load-bearing) experiment would trace outbound HTTP calls with a proxy during a simulated client-side read-timeout against a live Azure AI Foundry chat-completions deployment, for both azure-ai-inference and AzureOpenAI/openai-python clients, and diff the dependency counts. entries.name: Azure OpenAI: billing follows processing, not HTTP success — explicit 408-timeout and content-filter examples
entries.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim on learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/openai/faq (curl with a browser UA returned 107,258 bytes / 1,736 lines of real rendered content, not an SPA shell). This is squarely a documentation sentence: Azure's own FAQ asserting how its billing meter treats a request that reached and was processed by the service, regardless of the HTTP status code the client ultimately saw (408 timeout, 400 content-filter, or 200-with-content_filter finish_reason). The request left the customer's machine and reached the server in every named case; Azure is asserting its own billing behavior for that outcome. Per the bar, a documentation sentence caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY however plainly it reads — there is no measurement here confirming an invoice line item.
entries.savings: None claimed — this is the provider stating in its own words that failed (400/content-filter), timed-out (408), and content-filtered-after-success (200/finish_reason=content_filter) requests are billed in full whenever server-side processing occurred, closing off the 'it failed so I shouldn't pay' assumption. The mirror case (401 auth, 429 rate-limit) is explicitly not billed, because the service never began processing.
entries.provenance: curl with browser User-Agent against learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/openai/faq, 2026-08-18; real HTML returned (107KB), not a JS-only shell. entries.settlingExperiment: Needs a live Azure OpenAI resource: deliberately trigger (a) a content-filter block and (b) a client read-timeout set below actual generation time, then reconcile Azure Cost Management / usage-export line items for those specific request IDs against a normal successful call of equivalent prompt/output length. Not performed here — no API key, no live traffic.
entries.trap: A developer who treats a 408 or a content-filter 400 as 'nothing happened, safe to retry for free' pays twice for the same generation — once for the original processed-but-undelivered response, once for the retry — and Azure's own FAQ states this is expected behavior, not a billing bug worth disputing with support.

entries.name: Anthropic Tool Search Tool (defer_loading dynamic tool discovery, tool_search_tool_regex_20251119 / tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119)
entries.reasoning: Live-fetched anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use as raw HTML and grepped the load-bearing quote: 'Opus 4 improved from 49% to 74%, and Opus 4.5 improved from 79.5% to 88.1% with Tool Search Tool enabled.' matches exactly, 2 hits (rendered DOM + hydration JSON), matching the candidate's claimed quoteHits exactly. However the candidate's control-phrase count (claimed 4) does not hold up -- I measured 38 case-sensitive hits for 'Tool Search Tool' on the same raw dump, almost certainly because the page embeds the article twice (visible DOM plus a duplicate Sanity/Next.js hydration JSON payload) on top of genuine in-article repetition; the candidate's self-reported control count should not be trusted even though the load-bearing quote is solid. Separately, the mechanism paragraph presents 'excludes deferred tools from the system-prompt prefix' in quote marks as if lifted from the docs -- that exact fragment does NOT appear anywhere on the page (grepped and confirmed absent). The real sentence is: "Deferred tools aren't loaded into Claude's context initially. Claude only sees the Tool Search Tool itself plus any tools with defer_loading: false" -- substantively the same claim, actually a stronger and cleaner basis for it, but the candidate's phrasing was a paraphrase dressed as a quote, not a genuine quote (a lesser version of exactly the defect this sweep exists to catch, just not inside the graded 'quote' field). On the merits: this is a first-party, GA, named Anthropic feature whose own published benchmark shows tool-selection accuracy moving with the flag on/off (49%->74%, 79.5%->88.1%) -- that is direct evidence the model answers differently, not just that it costs less for an identical answer, which is a textbook FAIL under 'a different model answers.' Not a duplicate of dedupe-file entry 73 (mid-conversation tool_addition/removal cache-invalidation), which is a distinct claim about cache-prefix churn, not about this dynamic-discovery architecture.
entries.savings: Anthropic's cited 5-server example: ~55K-134K tokens of tool definitions collapse to ~8.7K tokens in context; but tool-selection accuracy on Anthropic's internal MCP eval moves from 49%->74% (Opus 4) and 79.5%->88.1% (Opus 4.5) with the feature on -- a capability delta bundled with the cost delta, not separable from it.
entries.provenance: Live fetch of https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use (raw HTML including Next.js hydration JSON), 2026-08-18.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit could see billed input tokens on tool-heavy turns drop sharply relative to the declared tools array size once defer_loading is set -- a visible token/schema-size mismatch requiring no content inspection. It cannot see, from outside, which specific tool definitions were or weren't expanded into context on a given turn without instrumenting the tool_search_tool result blocks.
entries.trap: Teams adopting Tool Search Tool purely to cut context-token cost, without re-running their own accuracy eval, are silently changing what the model can see and act on for any turn where it doesn't think to search -- Anthropic's own before/after numbers show the 'savings' and the capability change are the same mechanism, not two separable effects.
entries.settlingExperiment: Run an identical tool-heavy agent workload twice -- once with all tool definitions loaded eagerly, once with defer_loading + Tool Search Tool -- against a live API key, diffing both billed-token counts and task-success rate on an internal eval set. No API access in this sweep.

entries.name: Anthropic Programmatic Tool Calling (code_execution_20260120, Claude writes and runs orchestration code in a sandbox instead of exchanging raw tool-result JSON with the model)

The mechanism-field quote 'Tool results from programmatic calls are not added to Claude's context - only the final code output is' is a genuine contiguous statement in the source, not a splice: the source renders it as a bold span ('Tool results from programmatic calls are not added to Claude's context', 1 exact hit) immediately followed in the same sentence by plain text (' - only the final code output is') -- that's an HTML markup boundary within one sentence, not two fragments from different sentences stitched together, so it doesn't violate the no-splice rule. A feature whose own vendor reports it can make things worse on some workloads is not a uniform discount on an identical product -- it is a different product depending on call-pattern shape, which is the bar's FAIL condition. Correctly distinguished from dedupe entries 72 (generic MCP 'code mode') and 171 (parallel tool_use blocks) -- this is Anthropic's own first-party Messages-API feature with its own flag and its own numbers.

entries.name: Anthropic Structured Outputs — compiled-grammar cache (24h TTL, invalidated by schema/tool-set change, NOT by name/description edits)
entries.reasoning: Quote verified: 'Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use, making subsequent requests much faster' appears 2x (raw and tag-stripped), matching the claim, inside 'Grammar compilation and caching.' The adjacent 'Cache invalidation' bullets independently confirm the mechanism: invalidated by JSON-schema-structure or tool-set change; 'Changing only name or description fields does not invalidate the cache' -- matches the candidate's mechanism claim exactly. But the load-bearing behavioral claim -- that a cache hit and a cache miss apply byte-identical decode-time token masks, so nothing the model reads or produces changes -- is not something Anthropic states; it's the submitter's own inference (deterministic compile) layered on the provider's prose. Per the standing rule that a documentation sentence is the provider's word and caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY (only a measurement or a structural/open-source proof supports PASS_ABSOLUTE), and given no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/live traffic exists in this sweep and Anthropic's grammar compiler is closed/proprietary (unlike vLLM's PagedAttention or the published batch-invariant-kernels work, which earned PASS_ABSOLUTE on open/structural grounds), this is demoted from the submitter's proposed PASS_ABSOLUTE to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. Novelty vs existing id 91 independently confirmed: fetched OpenAI's own structured-outputs guide directly and found zero hits for 'system prompt', zero for '24 hour', and the only two 'cache' hits are unrelated SSE header boilerplate ('cache-control: no-cache') in bundled JS -- OpenAI's page documents no caching mechanism at all here, so the 24h TTL and the name/description invalidation exemption are genuinely Anthropic-specific facts this candidate adds.
entries.savings: Latency-only per Anthropic's own wording ('making subsequent requests much faster') -- no dollar or token figure stated anywhere on the page. Compute-reuse artifact, not a token discount: the injected format-explanation prompt (see next entry) still bills on every request regardless of grammar-cache hit or miss.
entries.provenance: Direct curl fetch of platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs (HTTP 200, 2.29MB). Quote grepped raw (2 hits) and HTML-tag-stripped with entities unescaped (2 hits) -- consistent. Control phrase 'JSON Schema' grepped both ways: 21 hits, matching the candidate's claim. Cross-checked OpenAI's structured-outputs guide via separate curl fetch (200, 2.55MB): 0 hits 'system prompt', 0 hits '24 hour', 2 unrelated 'cache' hits (JS boilerplate, not docs prose).
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit (request/response bytes only) could observe identical request tokens and output-token distributions across repeated calls with the same schema, with only a latency delta on the first post-change call vs. later ones. It could not observe or confirm the internal 24h TTL or the name/description invalidation exemption -- those are proprietary serving details stated only in documentation.
entries.trap: Treating Anthropic's grammar-cache description as measured fact rather than a documentation-only claim -- the 'hit and miss decode identically' identity assumption is the submitter's inference on top of the provider's words, not something Anthropic states or this sweep can measure.
entries.settlingExperiment: Send the same schema twice via the real API (cold vs. within-24h-cache), capture full logprobs/token-by-token output for a fixed prompt, and diff the decode-time token masks or output distributions between the cold and warm-cache calls. Requires a live ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, unavailable in this sweep.

entries.name: Anthropic Structured Outputs injects a real system prompt on every call — 'input token count is slightly higher', unconditionally
entries.reasoning: Quote verified: 'The injected prompt costs you tokens like any other system prompt' appears 2x (raw and tag-stripped), matching the claim, as the second of three bullets under the heading 'Prompt modification and token costs', directly following 'When using structured outputs, Claude automatically receives an additional system prompt explaining the expected output format.' This satisfies the bar's first clause literally: Anthropic states the model reads an entire additional system-prompt block, unconditionally, on every call using the feature, with no opt-out and no caching relief called out for this specific text. Novel vs id 146 (deliberate tool-schema trimming, a savings action) and id 179 (citations adding tokens, unrelated feature); OpenAI's structured-outputs guide has zero 'system prompt' hits, confirming this isn't a restatement of a cross-provider entry either.
entries.savings: None -- a documented cost. Anthropic states plainly: 'Your input token count is slightly higher' on every call using the feature. Someone assuming 'structured outputs = same prompt, just constrained decoding' is wrong by Anthropic's own text.
entries.provenance: Direct curl fetch, same page as prior entry. Quote grepped raw (2 hits) and tag-stripped (2 hits), matching claimed quoteHits:2. Control 'JSON Schema' verified at 21 hits both ways, matching claim.

One of the few candidates in this batch independently observable from usage-object token counts alone.
entries.trap: Assuming Structured Outputs is a free wrapper ('same prompt, just constrained decoding') and budgeting it at zero marginal input-token cost. Anthropic's own docs say otherwise: a real, additional system-prompt block is injected on every call, unconditionally, with no stated opt-out.
entries.settlingExperiment: Send matched request pairs (structured outputs on vs off, identical user content) through the real API and diff usage.input_tokens to quantify the injected-prompt overhead in actual tokens -- docs state direction (higher) but not magnitude.

entries.name: Anthropic: changing output_config.format busts the WHOLE conversation thread's prompt cache, not just the new turn

After stripping tags and unescaping entities, the exact sentence appears once (matching the claimed quoteHits:1), as the third bullet in the same list examined above -- confirmed by extracting ~3200 chars of tag-stripped context immediately preceding it and finding it directly follows the two bullets already verified under 'Prompt modification and token costs', not spliced from an unrelated section. entries.name: OpenAI: the structured-output JSON schema IS prompt content — key/property reordering alone 'can reduce cache reuse'
entries.reasoning: Quote verified: 'Changes to tool descriptions, parameter schemas, schema keys, or ordering can reduce cache reuse' appears exactly once (matches claimed quoteHits:1) in the section 'Keep tools and schemas identical', immediately preceded by 'Tool definitions, tool ordering, and structured output schemas contribute to the prompt prefix.' Control phrase 'prompt caching' case-sensitive: 23 hits, exactly matching claim; case-insensitive control separately checked at 45, confirming the candidate's stricter counting method.

entries.trap: Assuming a JSON schema's key order is cosmetic serialization detail, like the outer request envelope (id 143), and treating reordering keys or tidying descriptions as free refactoring. OpenAI's own docs say the schema is literally part of the cached prompt prefix -- reordering it is a content change, not a metadata change, and forfeits the cache discount on the next call.

The strict bar states a documentation sentence caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY 'however plainly it reads,' and that only a measurement or a structural argument that no request was ever sent supports PASS_ABSOLUTE. Neither applies here: a request unquestionably reaches the (closed-source, non-inspectable) embedding model, which runs inference regardless of the dimensions requested. The docs' code example showing a customer can truncate an already-returned full-dimension vector client-side proves the OUTPUT is mathematically consistent with prefix truncation -- it does not prove the DIRECT low-dimension API call performs the identical amount of server-side compute rather than some cheaper/early-exit path OpenAI or Voyage could run internally while still returning MRL-consistent results. Unlike vLLM/PagedAttention (open source, independently inspectable, PASS_ABSOLUTE elsewhere in this register), neither provider's inference server is open for inspection, so this rests entirely on the provider's own description of its internal pipeline -- textbook CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, not PASS_ABSOLUTE.
entries.savings: OpenAI's own MTEB example: text-embedding-3-large truncated to 256 dims still outperforms un-truncated ada-002 at 1536 dims (6x fewer floats). Voyage: 2048 -> 256 dims is 8x fewer floats, documented as 'a slight loss of retrieval quality.' The saving lands entirely downstream -- vector-DB storage, RAM, ANN search compute -- not on the embedding call's own billed input tokens, which are unaffected by the dimensions requested.

Checked existing-226.txt for 'embed|dimension|quantiz|matryoshka' -- only hits are #4 and #222, both about using an embedding as a cache KEY for chat-completion caching, an unrelated mechanism to producing the embedding vector itself. Confirmed novel axis.

entries.trap: Teams read 'shorten embeddings without losing concept-representing properties' and assume the dimensions parameter also cuts the embedding CALL's own cost -- it doesn't; billed input tokens for generating the embedding are unaffected by dimensions requested. The saving is real but lives entirely in downstream storage/search, not in the API bill for producing the vector.

entries.name: Output-dtype quantization for embeddings (Voyage AI int8 / uint8 / binary / ubinary)

entries.name: OpenAI distillation: fine-tune a smaller model on a larger model's captured outputs
entries.reasoning: Both quotes verified exactly against raw HTML. Primary: 'This technique can enable you to train a small model to perform similarly on a specific task to a larger, more costly model.' -- 1 hit at developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/supervised-fine-tuning, immediately preceded by the heading 'Distilling from a larger model' (1 hit, matching control). Secondary (cited by the candidate as separately verified): 'a smaller, cheaper, faster model' -- 1 hit at developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization, in the sentence 'You can train a smaller, cheaper, faster model to excel at a particular task where a larger model is not cost-effective.' Neither quote is spliced; both are contiguous and read in context exactly as the candidate represents them. This is an unambiguous FAIL under the bar's own definition -- 'a different model answers' -- and it does not even require trusting a vendor promise of identity, because the technique is definitionally the opposite: an offline training step produces a separate, smaller-weight artifact that is deployed to answer future requests in place of the original large model, and OpenAI is explicit the smaller model only 'performs similarly,' not identically. Distinct from entry #34 (async/batch, same model & weights) precisely because here the documented point of the feature is that the model itself changes.
entries.savings: No per-token discount on the same model. The saving comes entirely from swapping to gpt-4.1-mini's (or whichever smaller model's) base rate instead of gpt-4.1's -- confirmed via a second, independently-verified quote on OpenAI's model-optimization guide describing the explicit goal as training 'a smaller, cheaper, faster model,' not a cheaper way to run the same model.
entries.provenance: curl (raw HTML) of developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/supervised-fine-tuning (519,717 bytes) and developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization (353,047 bytes). Primary quote: grep -c exact match = 1. Control 'Distilling from a larger model': grep -c = 1. Secondary quote 'a smaller, cheaper, faster model': grep -c = 1, context confirmed via Python tag-strip extraction. Checked existing-226.txt for 'distill|fine.tun' -- zero hits; confirmed novel, no fine-tuning/distillation axis previously covered.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit watching only the `model` field in billed requests would see it change from the large model's ID to the small model's ID after a distillation/fine-tuning job completes -- a visible, permanent product swap, not a transient routing or caching artifact.
entries.trap: Teams call this 'the same task, cheaper' when it is 'a different, worse-at-everything-else model that OpenAI's own docs only claim performs similarly on the narrow distillation task' -- any drift in production traffic away from the distillation set's exact task shape degrades quality with no signal that the substitution occurred.
entries.settlingExperiment: Not applicable as an open question -- this is settled by the documented mechanism itself (a separate training run producing separate weights), not by a measurement this session lacks the means to run.

entries.name: LiteLLM streaming-usage reassembly drops cached_tokens, bills the cache hit as a full-price miss
entries.reasoning: Literally applying the bar's three questions, all are no: the model reads the same tokens, the same model answers, the same thinking happens — the defect is entirely in LiteLLM's local post-hoc cost arithmetic, downstream of anything that crossed the wire. But this register's own precedent treats billing/metering-integrity bugs that misrepresent real usage as FAIL regardless of whether model behavior itself changed (compare existing #67, the Anthropic '$16.6M ghost charge' billing glitch, and #153, gateway under/over-accounting on cut streams — both FAIL despite being pure accounting defects, not token-content changes). A cache-hit discount that the provider genuinely delivered gets silently negated by the metering layer and re-billed to the customer's own SpendLogs/budgets as if it never happened; treating that as anything but FAIL would treat a customer-facing overcharge as a pass. I did not broaden the bar's own token/model/thinking criteria to invent a new category — I followed the file's established treatment of this exact class of candidate.

entries.name: Helicone cache-write cost calculation ignores Anthropic's long-context pricing tier
entries.reasoning: Nothing about Anthropic's actual bill or the model's behavior is touched -- this is a bug in a third-party observability tool's own re-derivation of the invoice. I independently fetched Helicone's live `main` branch source (not just the issue's excerpt): packages/cost/models/calculate-cost.ts lines 218-227 compute cacheWrite5mCost/cacheWrite1hCost as `modelUsage.cacheDetails.write5m * basePricing.input * multiplier`, where `basePricing = preprocessedPricing[0]` (line 193) is hard-coded to the base/lowest tier, while input/output costs correctly call `getPricingTier(preprocessedPricing, getThresholdValue(...))` to pick the right tier (lines 207, 231). I then pulled authors/anthropic/claude-4.5-sonnet/endpoints.ts and confirmed the actual pricing config: threshold 0 -> input 0.000003 with cacheMultipliers write5m 1.25/write1h 2.0; threshold 200000 -> input 0.000006 (multipliers inherited). So on a >200k-token request, correct cache-write cost is 1.25x/2.0x of 0.000006, but the code always multiplies 1.25x/2.0x of 0.000003 -- exactly half, confirmed by source, not just claimed by the reporter. The issue itself is open with zero maintainer engagement (comments: []), but the defect is real and currently live in production source as of this fetch. Classified FAIL under this register's established metering-correctness precedent (cf. existing entry: 'Gateway-side under/over-accounting of provider-billed usage on cut streams' = FAIL) -- the tool's reported number does not match the real bill, even though no request, model, or token sequence changed. Flagging explicitly: this does not satisfy the bar's literal clause ('the model reads different tokens / a different model answers / different thinking happens') since nothing about the underlying Anthropic request changed -- the defect is purely in a downstream cost-estimator. I am following the register's own established broadened use of FAIL for metering/observability bugs rather than inventing a new bucket; if that precedent doesn't hold, this candidate might better be described as out-of-taxonomy rather than FAIL.
entries.savings: Underreport in the audit tool, not in Anthropic's real invoice: any Anthropic request over 200k tokens has cache-write cost displayed by Helicone at exactly half (not merely 'roughly half') of what Anthropic will actually bill, per the tier math I verified directly against the live pricing config. Customers who budget off Helicone's dashboard for long-context, cache-writing Anthropic traffic will be surprised by the real invoice. Open issue, unresolved, zero comments as of fetch.

entries.name: LiteLLM silently records $0.00 spend for any model missing a pricing entry, defeating budgets and chargeback
entries.reasoning: No effect on the model call itself. I independently fetched the actual PR diff (not just the description): the before state is `litellm.model_cost.setdefault(model_cost_key, {}).update(updated_dictionary)` in litellm/utils.py's register_model, called unconditionally during Router deployment registration; this materializes a bare `{}` key for any model absent from the public price catalog. `completion_cost()` treats key-presence as 'priced,' so lookups against that key return 0.0 instead of raising 'This model isn't mapped yet.' The fix wraps the mutation in `if updated_dictionary:` so an empty payload registers nothing, keeping the model 'unmapped' and the error loud. Two new tests in the diff (test_register_model_empty_payload_does_not_materialize_entry, test_router_init_without_pricing_keeps_unmapped_model_cost_loud) directly encode this before/after behavior with assertions matching the PR body's transcript. Same caveat as the other two: strictly, the completion itself, the model, and its token usage are all unaffected -- the defect is purely in the spend-accounting layer. FAIL applied per this register's established metering-correctness precedent for billing/observability-layer bugs, not the bar's literal token/model/thinking clause.

entries.name: AWS Bedrock bills a constant 36 input tokens for Llama 3.2 Vision regardless of the image's actual resolution
entries.reasoning: The customer-visible symptom is real and verified in the source table: Llama 3.2 11B returns exactly 36 input tokens for both 512x512 and 1120x1120 test images, while Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Nova Lite scale token count with resolution on the same platform (371->1531 and 1314->2610 respectively). This is an expected behavior for now' -- comes from a boto3 CONTRIBUTOR (adev-code) relaying what 'the Bedrock Service team has said' via an internal support ticket (Ref: P241706128), so it is one level of indirection from AWS's own engineers rather than a directly-quoted AWS statement or published doc page, but it is still the provider's own asserted mechanism for its own billing, delivered through a support channel -- exactly the scenario this register's own rule addresses ('a provider's own statement about its billing mechanics caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY even when delivered through a support thread rather than published docs'). I cannot independently verify AWS's internal preprocessing pipeline from outside their infrastructure -- there is no measurement or structural argument available to me that would support PASS_ABSOLUTE, and no evidence the model reads different tokens across calls (per AWS's account, it never does -- every image is genuinely resized to a fixed 240x240 before the model sees it), so FAIL does not apply either under the literal bar. CONTRACTUAL_ONLY is the correct cap. The issue itself is CLOSED (not open) as of fetch -- worth noting since the candidate doesn't claim otherwise, but flagging for accuracy.
entries.savings: No dollar delta claimed, and none is due here -- included as the inverse contrast case among the four: something that LOOKS like an undercounted/mis-metered bill (fixed 36 tokens regardless of image size, unlike Claude/Nova Lite on the same platform) but is asserted by the provider, via a support channel, to correctly reflect a fixed internal 240x240 resize baked into the model's own preprocessing. entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit (timing/token-count metadata only) could observe a compute/latency signature consistent with prefix caching — shorter processing time and fewer newly-processed tokens on requests sharing a prefix with recent traffic — but cannot observe the nondeterminism itself; confirming outputs actually diverge requires reading and diffing generated content across runs, which a content-blind audit by definition cannot do.
entries.trap: A team benchmarking a llama.cpp-served model for reproducibility with cache_prompt left at its default (true) will see occasional unexplained answer drift on requests sharing a prefix with recent traffic, misattributed to sampling/seed rather than to which batch-size code path served the shared prefix — and the fix (cache_prompt=false) silently forfeits the entire compute saving the feature exists for.

entries.name: vLLM Sleep Mode (enable_sleep_mode / /sleep /wake_up)
entries.reasoning: Quote verified exact, 1 hit (grep -F) in docs/features/sleep_mode.md. Control phrase 'enable_sleep_mode' 2 hits. Read the full 5,770-byte document, not just the quoted sentence, and found a nuance the candidate's mechanism text overstated: Level 1 sleep backs weights up in CPU RAM and restores them bit-for-bit on wake — a clean identity guarantee. Level 2 discards weights entirely and reloads via collective_rpc('reload_weights'), but the docs state Level 2 is explicitly used either (a) to reload the same weights from the original checkpoint when there isn't enough CPU RAM to back them up, or (b) 'to run a different model or update the model... e.g. RLHF weight update' — i.e., Sleep Mode's own API is deliberately dual-purpose and does NOT, as a blanket matter, guarantee weight identity across every sleep/wake cycle the way the candidate's mechanism paragraph claimed ('Either path resumes generation against the identical weights'). That said, the specific claim actually under audit — the quoted 'cost-saving scenarios where GPU resources need to be freed between inference workloads' — is the same-model pause/resume use case, where identity is structurally preserved (CPU-RAM backup, or reload from the unchanged original checkpoint). The RLHF weight-update path is a separately-labeled, intentional model change, not marketed as a free/equivalent-output saving, so it doesn't contaminate the specific savings claim being tested. PASS_ABSOLUTE holds for the claim as quoted; the dual-use gap is flagged below rather than silently dropped.
entries.savings: Frees up to 90%+ of GPU memory during idle periods (explicitly named for RLHF/training/cost-saving use) without re-downloading or re-quantizing weights on resume — the customer's own vLLM server toggling its own idle-cost lever.
entries.provenance: Fetched https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/vllm/main/docs/features/sleep_mode.md via curl (HTTP 200, 5,770 bytes) and read it in full (not just the quoted line). Grepped fixed-string for the exact candidate quote — 1 hit. Grepped for control phrase 'enable_sleep_mode' — 2 hits. Verified repo vllm-project/vllm via GitHub API: 89,376 stars, last push 2026-08-19T01:04:11Z, not archived.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit of the token wire sees nothing during sleep (no requests in flight) and no difference in the resumed request's tokens; the only observable signal is out-of-band infra telemetry — GPU memory occupancy dropping by 'up to 90%+' on /sleep and returning on /wake_up.
entries.trap: Sleep Mode's /wake_up and reload_weights primitives are dual-use: the same Level-2 path vLLM recommends for pure cost-saving pause/resume is also its documented mechanism for RLHF weight updates (loading genuinely different weights). The API doesn't distinguish the two intents at the wire level — a team that treats 'we called wake_up' as proof the model is unchanged, without separately confirming which checkpoint reload_weights pointed at, can silently serve stale or wrong weights if inference-serving and training infra ever share a Sleep-Mode-enabled deployment.
entries.settlingExperiment: With GPU access: hash model weight tensors before /sleep and after /wake_up for Level 1, and for Level 2 used without an intervening reload_weights call, confirming bit-for-bit identity; separately audit any Level-2 usage to confirm reload_weights was never pointed at a different checkpoint than the one active before sleep — not performed here, no GPU/vLLM runtime in this sandbox.

entries.name: Subagent resume via SendMessage drops system messages, invalidates cached prefix (Claude Code #86876)
entries.reasoning: Downgrade from proposed FAIL. Verified via `gh issue view 86876 --repo anthropics/claude-code`: real, OPEN issue, created 2026-08-15 — exactly 3 days before this sweep, matching the candidate's 'three days old' claim. Graded quote greps to exactly 1 hit, verbatim including the markdown bold markers, unspliced. Control-phrase count the candidate reported (3) is off — I count 4 occurrences of 'coordinator' in the body (the issue has zero comments, so body-only = total). Substantively this is weaker evidence than #29966: ZERO comments means zero maintainer acknowledgment and zero third-party corroboration — it is a single reporter's own raw-payload capture (methodologically careful, but entirely uncorroborated and unconfirmed by anyone else). As with the sibling candidate above, even taking the report at full face value this describes a cache-creation (recompute) event rather than a change to what tokens the model reads or what model answers — the same conversation content is ultimately resent and reprocessed, just uncached, which is a billing-inflation bug rather than a product-identity change under the bar's literal wording. Given single-source/zero-corroboration status, the categorical mismatch with FAIL's literal test, and no measurement performed in this sweep, I cannot settle this as FAIL.
entries.savings: 943,213 tokens of avoidable cache-creation billing in one 4-hour session, per the reporter's own raw-payload capture (OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES). Single-report, zero external corroboration, OPEN and unconfirmed by anyone including a maintainer.
entries.provenance: gh issue view 86876 --repo anthropics/claude-code --json title,body,state,comments,createdAt, fetched 2026-08-18. Issue OPEN, createdAt 2026-08-15T09:36:30Z, 0 comments, confirmed real. Quote hit count: 1 (exact, verbatim). Control phrase 'coordinator' hit count: 4 in the body — differs from the candidate's claimed 3.
entries.telemetrySignal: Partially visible to a content-blind audit: a spike in cache_creation_input_tokens relative to cache_read_input_tokens specifically on coordinator-to-subagent resume turns could in principle be flagged from usage telemetry alone. Confirming the root cause (dropped role:"system" messages) requires raw payload inspection — the reporter states the transcript itself cannot show this, only the outgoing payload can.
entries.trap: Teams running long multi-agent coordinator/subagent sessions who rely on cache economics to make that pattern affordable may be silently paying full cache-creation price on every coordinator-triggered subagent resume, with zero confirmation yet that Anthropic is even aware.
entries.settlingExperiment: Independent reproduction with OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES across a fresh multi-subagent session, comparing role:"system" message counts before/after a SendMessage-triggered resume — ideally by a second, unrelated party — is needed to move this past single-report status. Not performed in this sweep.

entries.name: Claude Code fork-mode default split: ON in interactive sessions (v2.1.232+), OFF in -p/Agent SDK, non-fork subagents get a separate cache lineage
entries.reasoning: Fetched https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents as raw HTML (1.13MB) and stripped tags for grep. The quote 'Claude Code turns fork mode on by default in interactive sessions and leaves it off by default in non-interactive mode with -p and in the Agent SDK.' is a genuine contiguous sentence in the rendered page -- I found it once (an inline <a> tag around 'non-interactive mode' breaks a raw-HTML grep, which is why the candidate's raw count would be 0; after stripping tags it's a clean single hit, not the 2 the candidate reported, likely from also matching the page's embedded JSX source blob -- not a splice, just a duplicate-in-file artifact, source is legitimate). Control phrase 'Separate cache' verified at exactly 2 hits, both from a table row: 'Prompt cache | Shared with main session | Separate cache' contrasting fork vs. non-fork subagents -- matches the candidate's claim. Cross-checked the two motivating GitHub issues cited in the mechanism: #29966 ('Agent SDK subagents have prompt caching disabled by default') and #86876 ('Resuming a subagent via SendMessage drops injected role:"system" messages, invalidating the cached prefix (943k tokens in one session)') both exist and are open, consistent with the docs' own admission that non-fork/off-default paths get a separate, uncached lineage. This is a documentation sentence describing the provider's own default configuration -- per the rule, that caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY regardless of how mechanistically plausible the described cache-sharing is. It refines rather than restates existing #202 ('fork subagents on-by-default'): #202 states the default unconditionally, while this source shows the default is conditional on session type (on only in interactive sessions, v2.1.232+; off in -p and the Agent SDK) and names the consequence for the off-path ('Separate cache'). That qualification is materially different information, not a restatement, so I am submitting it rather than dropping it.
entries.savings: No percentage stated by the docs. Verified verbatim in source: 'Because a fork's system prompt and tool definitions are identical to the parent, its first request reuses the parent's prompt cache. This makes forking cheaper than spawning a fresh subagent for tasks that need the same context.' No number attached.
entries.provenance: Anthropic first-party documentation (code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents), fetched and grepped directly as raw HTML per Rule 5, not converted markdown.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit reading only Anthropic's usage-object fields (cache_read_input_tokens vs cache_creation_input_tokens) per subagent request could observe the fork/non-fork split directly: fork-mode subagents' first request would show a cache-read hit matching the parent session's cache breakpoint, while non-fork subagents would show a fresh cache-creation event with no read -- but the audit could not tell from token counts alone whether it was run interactively or via -p/SDK; that requires seeing the invocation context.
entries.trap: A team building on the Agent SDK or running Claude Code headlessly via -p, having read that 'fork mode' shares the cache, will assume their subagent fan-out inherits the cache by default the way an interactive session does -- it does not, so every subagent spawn on that surface pays full cache-creation cost instead of the cheaper cache-read path, exactly the pattern issues #29966 and #86876 report.
entries.settlingExperiment: No live measurement was possible (no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no traffic). A settling experiment would run the identical subagent task twice with usage-object logging: once via /subtask in an interactive v2.1.232+ session, once via the Agent SDK with default config, and diff cache_read_input_tokens vs cache_creation_input_tokens on the subagent's first request across both paths.

entries.name: Anthropic's own multi-agent token multiplier: ~4x per single agent vs. one chat turn, ~15x for full multi-agent runs vs. chat
entries.reasoning: Fetched https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system as raw HTML (173KB) and grepped the stripped text. The quote 'agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats' is a genuine contiguous sentence -- confirmed at exactly 2 occurrences (grep -o | wc -l), matching the candidate's claim (raw HTML and stripped text both show it verbatim, with a duplicate elsewhere on the page, no splicing). Control phrase 'explains 80% of the variance' also confirmed at exactly 2 occurrences, in context: 'We found that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and the model choice as the two other explanatory variables' -- matches. Substantively: this is Anthropic disclosing, from its own production research-agent system, that an orchestrator-plus-subagents architecture reads a structurally larger number of tokens (each subagent independently re-reads its own system prompt/tools and performs its own exploration) and performs correspondingly more inference than a single chat completion. Applying the bar exactly as written -- 'does the model read a different sequence of tokens... If yes it is FAIL' -- this is an unambiguous yes: strictly more tokens are read and more generations happen, not the same computation redistributed. That the parenthetical example of FAIL is 'a changed product sold as a saving' does not gate the rule; the operative clause is unconditional, and this register's own precedent (e.g. existing #67 billing-glitch, #124 forgotten-cron-waste, #157 zombie-context) already uses FAIL for disclosed cost-increase/waste patterns that nobody marketed as savings. So FAIL stands even though Anthropic is transparent about it being a cost, not a saving.
entries.savings: Not a savings claim -- the opposite: Anthropic's own disclosed cost multiplier. Their framing: 'For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance.'
entries.provenance: Anthropic first-party engineering blog post reporting Anthropic's own internal measurement of their production multi-agent research system -- not our measurement, but the provider's own disclosed data, not a marketing claim of parity or savings.
entries.telemetrySignal: Directly observable by a content-blind audit: summed input+output+cache tokens per completed task, with no need to inspect any message content, would show roughly a 4x jump for a single-agent task vs. a single chat-turn baseline and roughly 15x for a full multi-agent orchestration run vs. the same chat baseline.
entries.trap: Teams adopting an orchestrator/subagent-fan-out pattern on the assumption that parallelizing work is 'free' (same total tokens, just split across workers) will instead see a bill 4-15x a single-chat baseline for comparable task value, and because per-subagent token counts each look individually reasonable, the multiplier only becomes visible at the aggregate invoice level.
entries.settlingExperiment: No live measurement was possible in this sweep (no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no traffic). A settling experiment would run one task as a single chat completion and the same task through an N-subagent orchestrator, summing every leg's usage-object token counts (input, output, cache creation, cache read) on both sides and comparing the ratio to the claimed 4x/15x.

entries.name: Workflow tool payload corruption causes 11-to-183 subagent spawn multiplication (Claude Code #75648)
entries.reasoning: Fetched via `gh issue view 75648 -R anthropics/claude-code`. Confirmed real: OPEN, filed 2026-07-08, single author (iaoiui), 0 comments, 0 reactions, no maintainer label or engagement as of 2026-08-18 -- six weeks with zero corroboration. Quote 'only 11 `agent()` calls were requested (via `parallel()` over 11 batches), but **183 actual sub-agent processes were spawned**' confirmed at exactly 1 occurrence in the issue body (matches candidate's claim). Control phrase 'TaskStop' actually occurs 6 times in the body, not the 3 the candidate reported -- the phrase is genuinely present and non-trivially discussed (a whole numbered symptom, 'TaskStop doesn't fully reach in-flight sub-agents', is devoted to it), so the control isn't broken, but the candidate under-counted it. Substantively, if true this is a clean FAIL under the bar (183 real spawned processes each reading tokens where 11 were requested is unambiguously 'the model reads a different sequence... more thinking happens'), but a single, uncorroborated, zero-engagement bug report describing an unidentified 'retry-or-duplicate-dispatch path' is not enough to confirm the mechanism actually occurred as described rather than, e.g., a reporter-side scripting artifact or an already-patched version-specific bug (filed against 2.1.204). INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE is the correct call, matching the candidate's own proposed verdict.
entries.savings: N/A -- a documented cost blowup, not a saving. Reporter's own estimate: ~7-10M tokens burned in under 10 minutes for what should have been 11 concurrent calls, a claimed ~16.6x spawn multiplication.
entries.provenance: Single open, unconfirmed GitHub issue (anthropics/claude-code#75648), 0 comments, 0 reactions as of this sweep -- verified directly via gh CLI, not secondhand.
entries.telemetrySignal: If real, a content-blind audit tracking only aggregate billed tokens (with no script-side expected-spawn baseline to compare against) would see nothing anomalous beyond 'unusually high usage' for that session -- the 11-requested-vs-183-spawned discrepancy is only visible to someone already comparing the workflow script's own call count against journal.jsonl's actual spawn count, which most billing-level audits would not do.
entries.trap: Teams building on the Workflow tool's dynamic agent()/parallel() fan-out with a moderately sized args payload (here ~13KB / ~105 small objects) could hit an uncapped spawn multiplier with no warning, since nothing in the tool appears to cap or alert on spawned-process count exceeding requested count -- and would not notice until the bill or the usage indicator spikes.
entries.settlingExperiment: Needs independent reproduction: rerun the reporter's exact repro shape (a ~13KB/~105-object args array through a parallel()-driven agent() fan-out) on a current Claude Code build with journal.jsonl spawn-count instrumentation, to confirm or refute the 11-to-183 multiplication. With zero maintainer or third-party engagement to date, this cannot be treated as confirmed.

entries.name: OTEL cost-usage counter double-counts across --resume processes sharing a session_id, inflating apparent spend >100x with zero real billing change (Claude Code #56317)
entries.reasoning: Fetched via `gh issue view 56317 -R anthropics/claude-code`. Confirmed real and well-corroborated: OPEN, filed 2026-05-05, 4 independent comments plus 3 thumbs-up reactions -- notably comment 3 (glockbender) supplies a deterministic two-process repro (`claude -p --session-id "$SID" ... &` run twice against the same SID) with byte-identical OTLP attribute maps arriving ~60ms apart, plus organization-wide 24-hour telemetry: 11.8% of users had at least one collided stream, 1.6% of streams affected, 1.34% of total cost hidden by the collision. Quote checked against the issue *title* (the candidate's quote is the literal title text) -- exact match, 1 occurrence, as claimed. Control phrase 'without a process-distinguishing label' confirmed at exactly 1 occurrence in the body, as claimed. Substantively: the collision is confined to the self-hosted OTEL exporter's missing pid/instance-id resource attribute on the claude_code_cost_usage_USD_total counter (and related token/active-time counters) -- the actual API requests sent to Anthropic, the model that answers them, and the true billed cost are all completely unaffected; only a locally-computed Prometheus-style aggregate is corrupted by attribute-collision. No request the customer's machine sends is duplicated, discarded, or reclassified -- this is purely a telemetry-emission bug downstream of billing, which is the structural argument the bar requires for PASS_ABSOLUTE (nothing on the wire to Anthropic changed).
entries.savings: N/A -- inverted framing: apparent >100x bill inflation visible only in a self-hosted monitoring dashboard, with zero actual change to billed tokens, requests, or the model that answered them. A measurement artifact, not a real multiplication.
entries.provenance: GitHub issue anthropics/claude-code#56317, OPEN, 4 comments including an independent deterministic repro and organization-scale quantified data, 3 thumbs-up reactions -- unusually well-corroborated for a single issue.
entries.telemetrySignal: This candidate IS itself about telemetry: a content-blind audit reading only the self-hosted OTEL cost counter would be actively misled into seeing a >100x runaway-cost event; the same audit reading Anthropic's own console/invoice total for the identical session would see no anomaly at all, since only the locally-derived counter is broken, not the provider's billing record.
entries.trap: Anyone doing cost oversight purely off self-hosted OTEL dashboards (rather than the provider's own invoice/console total) could conclude a large runaway-agent cost event occurred and trigger drastic response (kill switches, incident escalation) against a phantom -- and, worse, a real runaway-cost event happening concurrently on the same broken dashboard would be indistinguishable from the artifact.
entries.settlingExperiment: No further measurement needed to settle the wire-level claim: multiple independent reporters already isolated the bug to the OTEL exporter's label set (separate from the request/billing path), and one supplied a deterministic repro plus a direct diff against invoice-level totals showing the discrepancy is confined to the local counter. Any residual settling would just be reproducing glockbender's two-process `--session-id` repro against a current build to confirm the fix status.

entries.name: OpenAI Agents SDK nest_handoff_history compacts pre-handoff conversation into summary segments
entries.reasoning: Verified by direct curl fetch of https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/ (raw HTML, not WebFetch's summarizer) and grepped myself. Quote hit count: 1 (exact). Control phrase 'opt-in beta and is disabled by default while we stabilize it' hit count: 1 (exact), confirming this is off by default. Also independently grepped the mechanism's other embedded quote -- 'it's as though the new agent takes over the conversation, and gets to see the entire previous conversation history' -- 1 exact hit, describing the DEFAULT (flag-off) behavior the beta mode replaces. With the flag on, the docs describe a structural content substitution: summarizable history is replaced by generated <CONVERSATION HISTORY> segments; only items the docs classify 'lossless' survive verbatim. This is the provider's documentation directly asserting a token-sequence change (not asserting sameness), so FAIL is supported straight from the docs without needing a measurement. Repo checked per rule 7: openai/openai-agents-python, 28,752 stars, last pushed within the last day, not archived -- actively maintained, legitimate.
entries.savings: No percentage or dollar figure stated by the docs; framed as history/context management. The candidate correctly discarded an unsourced WebFetch-invented 'reduces token usage' framing that grepped at 0 hits -- good discipline, and I found no such framing either on direct fetch.
entries.provenance: Independently verified this session via direct curl (bypassing WebFetch's summarizing pass) against the live docs page.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit watching only per-turn request byte size / token counts to the handoff endpoint could see a drop in history size once the beta flag is enabled, but could not confirm from size alone that the drop is 'summarization' versus a genuinely shorter conversation -- needs either the content or knowledge of the flag state.
entries.trap: Adopting this for token savings trades fidelity for cost with no documented guarantee that summarization preserves task-relevant details beyond the narrow 'lossless' item carve-out -- an agent that later needs something summarized away fails silently, and nothing in the docs bounds how much gets compressed.
entries.settlingExperiment: Run one multi-agent handoff task twice (flag off vs on, same seed/temperature); diff the second agent's actual input token array against the full original transcript to quantify exactly how many original tokens were replaced by summary tokens, and compare task success/quality between the two runs.

entries.name: OpenAI consumer Terms of Use: account-credential-sharing ban
entries.reasoning: Direct curl fetch of https://openai.com/policies/terms-of-use/ returned only a Cloudflare JS-challenge shell (confirmed: body is the 'cdn-cgi/challenge-platform/h/g/orchestrate/chl_page' script, no article content) -- per rule 6, fell back to the Wayback Machine, which served a capture with an embedded wombat timestamp of 20260818161346, i.e. today. On that copy the quote 'You may not share your account credentials or make your account available to anyone else and are responsible for all activities that occur under your account.' is exact (found verbatim, appearing once in the rendered article plus once more in a duplicate Next.js hydration JSON blob -- a rendering artifact, not two different claims). It sits directly under an H2 heading reading 'Registration and access', confirming the control phrase. This is purely an account/access-layer restriction on who may originate a request under a login; the model call itself is unaffected. Per the bar, a documentation/ToS sentence caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY.
entries.savings: Splitting one paid ChatGPT account's login across multiple people to divide the subscription cost, as stated.
entries.provenance: Independently verified this session via a same-day Wayback Machine snapshot after the live fetch was blocked by a Cloudflare challenge.
entries.telemetrySignal: None on the token stream -- enforcement, if any, would rely on account-side signals (many devices/IPs on one login, concurrent-session counts), not on anything visible in request or response content.
entries.verifiedAgainst: 2026-08-18, Wayback Machine capture stamped 20260818161346 (same-day snapshot of openai.com/policies/terms-of-use/)
entries.trap: Treating this as a technical gray area rather than a contractual one -- it reads identically to splitting a Max-style subscription, and enforcement (account suspension) doesn't care that the underlying tokens were byte-identical.
entries.settlingExperiment: N/A for CONTRACTUAL_ONLY -- nothing about a ToS clause is settled by measuring model output; the only open question (how OpenAI detects/enforces sharing in practice) isn't a token-level fact this register can measure.

entries.name: OpenAI Services Agreement: API-key buy/sell/transfer ban

Live fetch hit the same Cloudflare challenge shell as the ToU page; fell back to a Wayback snapshot dated 2026-08-14 (4 days old) of services-agreement/. Quote 'buy, sell, or transfer API keys from, to, or with a third party' is exact, item (g) in a list of prohibited actions. Also independently grepped the mechanism's second embedded claim -- 'Customer will not share Account access credentials or individual login credentials between multiple users. Customer may not resell or lease access to its Account or any End User Account.' -- exact match, confirming the three-level structure (don't share login / don't resell account / don't trade key) the candidate describes. Doc header confirms 'Effective: January 1, 2026', so this is current text, not stale. Everything here operates at the credential/account-authorization layer -- the model call underneath is unaffected -- so it caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY.
entries.savings: Reselling or brokering OpenAI API keys/account access at a margin to third parties, as stated.
entries.provenance: Independently verified this session via a Wayback Machine snapshot dated 2026-08-14 of the redirect target (services-agreement/); live fetch was blocked by a Cloudflare challenge.
entries.telemetrySignal: None on the model/token side -- enforcement is a credential/billing-relationship check (does the account presenting a key match who provisioned it), invisible to anything reading request or response content.
entries.verifiedAgainst: 2026-08-14, Wayback Machine snapshot of openai.com/policies/services-agreement/ (redirect target of the cited business-terms/ URL); document header states Effective January 1, 2026
entries.trap: This clause is a direct kill switch on any margin-on-API-keys resale business model, not a theoretical edge case -- it names the exact commercial act (buy/sell/transfer keys) such a product performs.
entries.settlingExperiment: N/A for CONTRACTUAL_ONLY -- this is a flat contractual prohibition; no model measurement would change the verdict.

entries.name: Google APIs Terms of Service: credential confidentiality is a 'reasonable efforts' duty, not an absolute ban
entries.reasoning: Direct curl fetch of https://developers.google.com/terms succeeded (real content, no JS wall). Grepping the RAW, unmodified HTML for the submitted quote returns 0 hits -- the source's raw markup line-wraps mid-phrase ('keep your / credentials confidential'), which is exactly the failure mode rule 3 is designed to catch, so flagging it rather than passing the 0 through. Re-checked with only whitespace normalized (collapsing HTML line-wraps, not joining separate sentences or sections): the quote is a single, genuinely contiguous run -- 1 hit -- inside one list item, under the H3 'b. Confidential Matters'. Note this is a DIFFERENT subsection than 'a. API Prohibitions' (which does hit twice for the control phrase) -- the credentials duty and the flat sublicense ban are sibling clauses under 'Section 4: Prohibitions and Confidentiality', not the same clause. Independently confirmed the mechanism's other claim -- that Section 4a bars sublicensing outright: 'Sublicense an API for use by a third party. Consequently, you will not create an API Client that functions substantially the same as the APIs and offer it for use by third parties' -- exact match. Page footer states 'Last modified: November 9, 2021', confirming this is still the live, unchanged current text as of today's fetch, not a stale cache. A duty-of-reasonable-effort standard is a real distinction from OpenAI's/AWS's flat prohibition, but it's still a documentation sentence describing a legal standard -- caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY.
entries.savings: Sharing one set of Google API developer credentials across multiple users/projects instead of provisioning separate keys, as stated.
entries.provenance: Independently verified this session via direct fetch (no SPA/challenge issue on this page). Flag: the submitted quote scores 0 on a literal raw-HTML grep because of an in-source line wrap inside the sentence, not because of a splice or dropped table cell -- confirmed genuine and contiguous only after whitespace normalization, and reporting that nuance rather than silently accepting the submitted quoteHits:1.
entries.telemetrySignal: None -- 'reasonable efforts to prevent and discourage' is a subjective standard assessed after the fact (e.g. in a dispute), not something request-level telemetry could check in real time.
entries.verifiedAgainst: 2026-08-18, direct fetch of developers.google.com/terms; page states 'Last modified: November 9, 2021'
entries.trap: Reading 'reasonable efforts' as license to share credentials loosely is the trap -- it's a lower bar than OpenAI's or AWS's flat ban, but still a breach if efforts were plainly inadequate, and it sits in the same section as an unconditional, unrelated ban on sublicensing API access to a third party.
entries.settlingExperiment: N/A for CONTRACTUAL_ONLY -- 'reasonable efforts' is a legal standard assessed after the fact in a dispute, not something request-level telemetry or a model measurement could settle.

entries.name: Google Cloud Platform Terms of Service: naming multi-account use to dodge fees/quotas as a defined prohibition
entries.reasoning:
Quote verified as an exact, contiguous match against the live page: 1 hit after normalizing HTML whitespace (raw `grep -o` reports 0 only because the phrase is line-wrapped across ~6 lines of indented markup inside a

tag, not because it is spliced from elsewhere — confirmed by reading 1400 chars of surrounding context, which shows the clause running on as one unbroken sentence: '...in a manner intended to avoid incurring Fees (including creating multiple Customer Applications, Accounts, or Projects to simulate or act as a single Customer Application, Account, or Project (respectively)) or to circumvent Service-specific usage limits or quotas...'). Control phrase 'Service Specific Terms' = 12 hits, matching the claim exactly. This is a real, specific, current ToS clause explicitly naming the multi-account/multi-project topology trick and banning it. It changes nothing about what tokens a model reads — it is a policy statement about account structure, sourced entirely from documentation. Per the bar, a documentation sentence caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY regardless of specificity. Not a restatement of anything in the existing 226-entry register (entry 191/'Team/Enterprise per-seat pricing as sanctioned alternative to account sharing' is adjacent but a different provider and a different clause).
entries.savings: Spinning up multiple free-tier or separately-billed GCP accounts/projects and spreading traffic across them to duck per-account rate limits or fees
entries.provenance: Fetched https://cloud.google.com/terms/ as raw HTML via curl (836,615 bytes, HTTP 200). Page shows 'Last modified June 1, 2026' — about 2.5 months old at the 2026-08-18 check date, still the current live terms.
entries.telemetrySignal: None available to a content-blind audit. Multi-account/multi-project structure is visible in account metadata, but the clause turns on intent ('in a manner intended to avoid incurring Fees') — a content-blind observer sees the same topology whether it's legitimate cost-center separation or fee-avoidance, and can't tell which from wire traffic alone.
entries.trap: Reads like a narrow anti-fraud clause but is written broadly enough to catch ordinary cost-motivated project-splitting — any customer who reorganizes GCP projects partly to land in a friendlier fee/quota bracket is now arguably inside a clause Google can invoke, even absent bad-faith intent.
entries.settlingExperiment: None settles a contract-boundary claim — only an actual GCP enforcement action against a specific account topology would show where 'intended to avoid Fees' is drawn in practice; nothing here was or could be measured this session.

entries.name: AWS Customer Agreement: credential/key trading ban with an explicit subcontractor carve-out
entries.reasoning: Quote verified as an exact, contiguous match — but it occurs TWICE in the fetched page (byte offsets 241,727 and 300,050 in the whitespace-normalized text), not once as claimed. Both occurrences carry identical surrounding text and the same 'Last Updated: August 14, 2026' stamp, which points to a page-level DOM duplication artifact (the whole agreement appears to be rendered twice in the source), not a splice or two different clauses — the substance of the quote is unaffected and genuinely present verbatim. Control phrase 'Log-In Credentials and Account Keys' likewise hit 2 (not 1). Correcting the candidate's hit-count claim, the clause itself checks out: real, current, unambiguous ban on selling/transferring/sublicensing AWS credentials, with an explicit exception for agents/subcontractors doing the customer's own work. Docs-only sourcing caps this at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY per the bar; nothing about model tokens is implicated one way or the other. No duplicate in the existing 226-entry register (which has no AWS credential-sharing clause).
entries.savings: Selling or subletting AWS account credentials/access keys (which would also authenticate Bedrock model calls) to a third party
entries.provenance: Fetched https://aws.amazon.com/agreement/ as raw HTML via curl (530,417 bytes, HTTP 200). 'Last Updated: August 14, 2026' — 4 days old at the 2026-08-18 check date, current. The quote and control phrase each appear twice in source, both instances identical, consistent with a duplicated content block rather than conflicting versions.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit could observe multiple distinct client IPs/user agents authenticating with one shared credential set over time — but that traffic shape is identical whether it's prohibited resale or the explicitly permitted subcontractor case, so telemetry alone cannot distinguish them; only knowing the relationship between the parties resolves it, and that isn't a wire-observable fact.
entries.trap: The subcontractor exception covers someone doing the customer's own work, not someone the customer sells access to — a reseller who reads 'agents and subcontractors performing work on your behalf' as covering their paying end-customers is stretching a narrow B2B-outsourcing carve-out into a resale license it doesn't grant.
entries.settlingExperiment: None — whether a given relationship counts as 'performing work on your behalf' is a legal reading (or an actual AWS enforcement decision) for a specific fact pattern, not something an API measurement can settle.

entries.name: Microsoft Online Services Product Terms: 'Multiplexing' — pooling access doesn't reduce what you owe
entries.reasoning: Quote and control phrase both verified as exact, single (1) contiguous matches against the live page, matching the claim exactly. Full surrounding context confirms the described mechanism precisely: the Multiplexing clause lists pooling/connection-reduction/access-reduction methods, then closes with the flat sentence quoted here — it is the final clause of a definition, not an accounting rule bolted on from elsewhere. This is again purely documentation — an assertion about license accounting, not a technical claim about model behavior — so it caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY under the bar. Genuinely distinct in structure from the GCP/AWS entries in this batch: Microsoft doesn't prohibit the conduct, it just refuses to let it reduce the license count owed. No prior entry in the 226-file register touches Azure/Microsoft account-sharing or multiplexing terms at all.
entries.savings: Using a shared connection pool/automation layer so fewer named users or devices appear to access an Online Service directly, in order to license fewer seats
entries.provenance: Fetched https://www.microsoft.com/licensing/terms/product/ForallOnlineServices/all as raw HTML via curl (202,536 bytes, HTTP 200, fully server-rendered — no SPA-shell problem). The page's effective-date picker lists 8/10/2026 as current, 8 days old at the 2026-08-18 check date.
entries.telemetrySignal: A content-blind audit CAN observe the shape of multiplexing itself — fewer distinct authenticated sessions/connections hitting the backend than there are real end users, the classic connection-pooling signature. What it cannot observe is whether the customer purchased the correct (larger) license count behind that pool — that's an account/billing fact, not visible in request traffic.
