verdicts.name: Google Cloud Flexible Savings Plan (FSP) — spend-based committed-use discount covering Gemini Enterprise / Vertex AI generative-AI usage
verdicts.reason:
Independently re-fetched docs.cloud.google.com/docs/cuds-flexible-savings-plans as raw HTML (201KB, curl, no JS shell issue) and re-verified every load-bearing claim myself rather than trusting the candidate's report.

Quote fidelity (rule 3/4 check): candidate's cited quote "the system monitors your usage and applies the applicable consumption model rates" is a real, contiguous substring — quoteHits=1/1 — but only after correct whitespace normalization; a naive line-mode grep gives a false 0 because the source HTML breaks that sentence across a line inside the paragraph ("...term. The system monitors your usage and\napplies the applicable consumption model rates.\n\n"). Python substring match on normalized text: 1 hit. Control phrase "How Flexible Savings Plans work": controlHits=1/1. No splice — single contiguous run, capitalization aside. This is a genuine pass, not a fabrication like the 22%-defective ones the sweep flagged.

Mechanism check (my lens): confirmed via full-page text dump that FSP is defined as "a type of spend-based committed use discount (CUD)" — commit a fixed $ amount for a 1- or 3-year term; "the billing system evaluates your usage and applies the FSP discounts on an hourly basis"; overage is "billed at the standard on-demand rate"; discount is applied "proportionally to all costs." I grepped the full normalized page for capacity/reservation language that would push this into the Provisioned-Throughput bucket (provisioned, GSU, dedicated, throughput, capacity, priority, SLA, routing, guarantee) — zero hits on all. No discount percentage is stated anywhere (zero N% matches) — matches candidate's unquantified-savings framing.

Scope check (the one place I expected to catch an overclaim): the FSP landing page itself never says "Vertex AI" — it only says "Gemini Enterprise FSP applies to Google Cloud generative AI models and product offerings," which looked like a possible title overclaim bundling a packaged product (Gemini Enterprise) with the separate developer API (Vertex AI). I followed the page's own link to the "Gemini Enterprise Flexible Savings Plan Eligible SKUs" table (cloud.google.com/skus/sku-groups/...) and confirmed it: "Vertex AI" is a listed Service Name in that table with hundreds of eligible SKU rows for actual token-metered generative-model usage (Gemini 2.0/2.5/3 Input/Output Text/Image/Audio, caching SKUs) — not just AutoML or the packaged search product. So the candidate's scope framing is accurate, not an overclaim; no narrowing needed.

Applying the bar: the request that leaves the customer's machine (a normal Vertex AI / Gemini Enterprise API call) is structurally unmodified by FSP — FSP is a monthly-commitment ledger with an hourly rate lookup applied at the billing layer, after metering, with no capacity/priority/routing hook into the serving path (unlike PT/GSU, which this register already correctly holds at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, e.g. id96/id100/id113). This is the same structural shape as three entries already resident in this register at PASS_ABSOLUTE — id110 (Anthropic Enterprise committed-spend), id102 and id114 (AWS Marketplace private offers drawing down committed spend) — i.e. dollars-only arithmetic that by definition (spend-based vs. resource-based CUD) cannot touch tokens, model, or thinking budget, so it clears via the bar's "structural argument that no request was ever sent [differently]," not via trusting an unverifiable behavioral assertion. Confirmed against existing-226.txt: no FSP/Flexible Savings Plan entry present under any name — not a duplicate.

I find no defect in quote, no scope overclaim, and correct mechanism classification consistent with register precedent. Verdict stands: PASS_ABSOLUTE, upheld, same name.

verdicts.name: Bedrock AgentCore Runtime microVM active-consumption billing
verdicts.proposedName: Bedrock AgentCore Runtime microVM active-consumption billing (CPU/memory hosting meter for the agent's own orchestration container, structurally disjoint from the separately-billed model-invocation payload)
verdicts.reason:
Independently re-verified, not trusting the candidate's own numbers or the AI-summarized WebFetch. Curled raw HTML from https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/ (200, 515KB), stripped tags to plain text, then grepped:
- Full contiguous quote "...typically spend 30-70% of time in I/O wait (waiting for LLM responses, tool / API calls, or database queries). With pre-allocated pricing, you would pay for idle CPU during these wait periods. With the active resource consumption-based pricing in AgentCore Runtime, I/O wait and idle time is free..." = 3 hits, and confirmed by inspecting the surrounding text that all three sentences run on with no other text between them in the source — this is a real contiguous paragraph (trimmed at both ends), not a splice of fragments from different places.
- Control phrases "you only pay for active resource consumption" / "active resource consumption-based pricing" / "30-70%" = 9 hits each. Both counts match the candidate's stated "quote x3, control x9" exactly, so the original verification was done honestly, not fabricated.

Mechanism check (my lens): AgentCore Runtime meters CPU (active-only, idle/I/O-wait free) and memory (peak-usage regardless of active/idle — confirmed 18x: "peak memory consumed up to that second," a nuance the candidate didn't surface but that doesn't touch the bar) of the microVM hosting the agent's own orchestration code, at per-second granularity. This meter has no path to the model-invocation payload in any Runtime configuration: the LLM call is a network request the microVM makes and waits on (I/O wait, by the source's own framing), billed separately per-token by whichever model provider is called. Even the edge case of a self-hosted model running inside the container remains content-blind, since CPU cycles are counted, not tokens. The one real caveat — AWS's internal active-vs-idle CPU detection ("if no other background process is running") is not independently auditable — bears on billing *accuracy*, not on whether the model reads different tokens, so it doesn't cap the verdict below PASS_ABSOLUTE. This is actually a cleaner PASS_ABSOLUTE than most register entries in this class (e.g. JSON-envelope-reordering cases): those touch the wire in a content-blind way, this billing axis never touches the wire at all — it's an entirely separate charging dimension, not a transform of the request. No narrowing needed; original verdict stands.

verdicts.name: Bedrock Custom Model Import: scale-to-zero Custom Model Unit billing
verdicts.proposedName: AWS Bedrock Custom Model Import: 5-minute-window / scale-to-zero billing metering
verdicts.reason:
Not a duplicate of existing-226.txt (no CMI/scale-to-zero entry there).

Quote fidelity checks out. Independent fresh fetch (curl, UA-spoofed, private path, 890,765 bytes — matches the candidate's reported 890KB) of https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/ confirms: control 'Custom Model Unit' = 70 hits (matches candidate exactly), 'Custom Model Import' = 4 hits (matches), and both plausible quote strings — "You are billed in 5-minute windows for the duration your model copy is active" and "If there are no invocations for a 5-minute period, Bedrock will scale down to zero and scale back up when you invoke your model" — each hit exactly 3 times (accordion repeats per model family: Llama, Mistral, Mixtral, Flan), matching the candidate's reported "quote x3". No quote fabrication or splicing here — this part of the candidate's work is solid and independently reproduced.

The verdict is where it fails under the mechanism lens. Everything in this claim — the 5-minute billing window, the scale-to-zero trigger, the cold-start reload, and the premise that "AWS never touches the weights' content" — comes from one source: the AWS pricing page prose. Per the register's own rule, "A documentation sentence is THE PROVIDER'S WORD, however plainly it reads, and caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. Only a measurement, or a structural argument that no request was ever sent, supports PASS_ABSOLUTE." There is no measurement here — no AWS credentials, no live invocation of a CMI-hosted model, nothing observed about actual cold-start behavior, actual metering-window boundaries, or actual serving fidelity. This sweep states plainly it has no live traffic.

The candidate's attempt to clear CONTRACTUAL_ONLY is a "structural argument": model substitution is "logically impossible, since AWS never touches the weights' content." That premise is not independently verified — it's read off the same page, and the same page contradicts it. The on-demand pricing paragraph states the per-copy throughput/concurrency limit "depends on factors such as input/output token mix, hardware type, model size, architecture, inference optimizations, and is determined during the model import workflow" (verified: "inference optimizations" hits 3x, same 3 accordion copies as the quote). AWS explicitly documents applying inference optimizations during import — this is a standard industry practice (quantization, kernel fusion, compilation) that means the served artifact is not guaranteed byte-identical to the uploaded weights. That's an unexamined dependency the candidate's "never touches the weights' content" claim glossed over, and it directly undercuts the "even stronger than AgentCore" argument.

Separately: the candidate's "AgentCore entry" comparator does not appear anywhere in the 226-line existing register I was given, so it cannot be used as an established precedent here.

Closer, actually-on-point precedent already sits in the register and points the other way: existing id 34, "Async/batch billing path — 50% discount vs synchronous API, same model & weights," is CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. That is structurally the same shape of claim (provider says "your unmodified model/weights, just billed differently") and the register already declined to give it more than CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. Nothing about CMI's scale-to-zero mechanism is more independently verifiable than that.

Net: the request genuinely leaves the customer's machine on every invocation, and everything about what answers it, how long cold-start takes, and how the 5-minute clock is metered rests entirely on AWS's asserted, unmeasured description of its own infrastructure. That's the definition of CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, not PASS_ABSOLUTE.

verdicts.name: Microsoft Agent Prepurchase Plan (Agent Commit Units / ACU) discount tiers
verdicts.proposedName: Microsoft Agent Prepurchase Plan (ACU) discount tiers — scoped to Microsoft Foundry model-API usage and Copilot Credit-eligible usage (Copilot Studio, Dynamics 365 first-party agents, Copilot) only; does NOT cover Microsoft Fabric or GitHub
verdicts.reason:
Independently re-fetched both sources as RAW HTML (not markdown) per rule 5, since the first WebFetch pass silently dropped table structure exactly the way the rules warn about.

CORE MECHANISM HOLDS. Raw HTML of azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/microsoft-foundry/ (the ai-foundry URL 301s here — product was renamed) confirms the tier table verbatim in <td> cells: 1|20,000|5%, 2|100,000|10%, 3|500,000|15% (each value greps 1/1 hit). "Agent Commit Units" hits exactly 2 on that page, matching the candidate's controlHits. The worked example — "if Microsoft Copilot Studio generates a retail cost of $100... then 100 Agent CUs (ACUs) are consumed" — is present verbatim and is the load-bearing sentence: it shows retail cost is computed FIRST by the product's own normal metering, and ACU balance is decremented from that already-computed dollar figure. That is a downstream currency-conversion, structurally the same shape as the register's existing PASS_ABSOLUTE committed-spend precedents (#110, #114, #118, #120, #194), not a "no request was sent" case but a "request sent, priced normally, paid via prepaid balance instead of cash" case — which this register has already and repeatedly accepted past CONTRACTUAL_ONLY for single-metering-path billing substitutions. Found no mechanism anywhere in either document by which holding an ACU plan changes routing, deployment, or model selection.

TWO REAL DEFECTS IN THE CANDIDATE'S SUPPORT, NEITHER FATAL TO THE VERDICT:

1. Splicing (Rule 4 violation, confirmed twice). Fetched learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/reservations/agent-pre-purchase raw HTML (note: the candidate's own cited URL under ai-foundry/agents/concepts 404s — this is the real location). The "combine" quote splices two different sentences: actual text is "Pre-purchase plan discounts don't combine with other discounts you might have. If you have additional discounts, the pre-purchase plan discount is applied independently, which may result in a lower effective discount rate..." — the candidate's "..." silently drops a full sentence. The "consumed first" quote is worse: "Reservations always apply before prepurchase plans." is a standalone bolded callout heading; "When you have both a reservation... the reservation discount is always consumed first." is the following, separate paragraph sentence. The candidate joined heading + paragraph with an ellipsis — precisely the "different sentences or sections" splice Rule 4 names.

2. False coverage claim, self-contradicted by the candidate's own better-sourced quote. The candidate asserts "ACU covers 'Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft Fabric, and GitHub' per the Learn doc's title/lede" — but that's the ARTICLE's SEO title (the article surveys four separate instruments: Foundry PTU reservations, Fabric Capacity reservations, a Copilot Credit-only prepurchase plan, AND the Agent/ACU plan). The doc's actual benefit-precedence table states, twice, that "Microsoft Agent Prepurchase Plan... Applied last to remaining AI usage across all platforms — Broader coverage for heterogeneous AI workloads for Copilot Credit and Microsoft Foundry usage" (verbatim), and separately: "Your Microsoft Agent prepurchase plan automatically uses your ACUs to pay for eligible Copilot and Microsoft Foundry usage" (verbatim). Fabric has its own separate Capacity reservation; GitHub isn't in the ACU mechanism at all (it appears only in nav/meta/title, 4 raw hits, none in the actual benefit-application mechanics). This directly contradicts the pricing page's own overview sentence that the SAME candidate quoted correctly earlier ("save on Microsoft Foundry and Copilot Credit costs... across the included Microsoft services") — an internal self-contradiction the candidate should have caught by reading the doc body instead of stopping at the title.

NET EFFECT ON THE VERDICT: narrowing scope to what ACU actually covers (Foundry + Copilot Credit-family) makes the PASS_ABSOLUTE argument cleaner, not weaker — both covered products are metered-request services following the identical "compute retail cost via normal metering, then draw ACU" pattern; the two products the candidate wrongly folded in (Fabric capacity/throttling, GitHub) are exactly the kind of structurally-different mechanisms a MECHANISM-lens review should worry about, and they turn out not to be in scope at all. No routing/model-selection dependency was found unexamined once the false 4-product claim is corrected.

Everything here is documentation-only — no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no measured Azure invoice, consistent with the sweep's no-live-traffic constraint. That caps the finding at what the register's own precedent already treats as acceptable for pure billing-substitution claims (PASS_ABSOLUTE by structural argument about where the discount sits in the pipeline, not by taking Microsoft's word for "nothing changed").

verdicts.name: Microsoft Agent Prepurchase Plan (Agent Commit Units / ACU) discount tiers
verdicts.proposedName: Microsoft Agent Prepurchase Plan (ACU) discount tiers — PASS_ABSOLUTE only where ACU is redeemed against standard pay-as-you-go metered usage; CONTRACTUAL_ONLY where redeemed against Microsoft Foundry PTU-priced usage
verdicts.reason:
Confirmed 226 is the last existing id (candidate is new, not a resubmission). Fetched raw HTML of azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/ai-foundry/ (216,949 bytes) — the primary facts check out cleanly: "Agent Commit Units" hits exactly 2 (matches candidate's controlHits=2), and the tier table is verified verbatim in the raw HTML — Tier 1: 20,000 ACU / $19,000 (5% off $20,000 face value), Tier 2: 100,000 ACU / $90,000 (10% off), Tier 3: 500,000 ACU / $425,000 (15% off) — exact match to the candidate's 20K/5%, 100K/10%, 500K/15% claim. The pricing page's own footnote also gives clean, non-spliced support for the downstream-accounting framing: "If Microsoft Copilot Studio generates a retail cost of $100 based on Copilot Credit and Microsoft Foundry usage, then 100 Agent CUs (ACUs) are consumed" — retail cost is computed first, ACU is drawn down after.

But the candidate's two "Also independently confirmed... this session" quotes from the companion Learn doc (I resolved the correct URL via the pricing page's own footnote link: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/reservations/agent-pre-purchase, HTTP 200, 63,148 bytes) are BOTH spliced — this is the exact defect pattern HARD RULE #4 forbids and the exact rhetorical framing ("independently verified/confirmed this session") the sweep singled out as having produced two of its worst entries.

Splice 1 (non-stacking): candidate quotes 'Pre-purchase plan discounts don't combine with other discounts... applied independently, which may result in a lower effective discount rate' as one unit. Verified programmatically: that joined string does not appear verbatim anywhere in the doc. The real, contiguous sentence is: "Pre-purchase plan discounts don't combine with other discounts you might have. If you have additional discounts, the pre-purchase plan discount is applied independently, which may result in a lower effective discount rate than the listed tier percentage." The candidate's ellipsis silently drops "you might have. If you have additional discounts, the pre-purchase plan discount is" — joining fragments of two different sentences.

Splice 2 (PTU-first waterfall): candidate quotes 'Reservations always apply before prepurchase plans... the reservation discount is always consumed first. Only usage that exceeds the reservation quantity draws from prepurchase plan commit units' as one unit. Verified: not a contiguous substring. Real text: "Reservations always apply before prepurchase plans. When you have both a reservation (such as Microsoft Foundry PTU or Fabric Capacity) and a prepurchase plan covering the same usage, the reservation discount is always consumed first. Only usage that exceeds the reservation quantity draws from prepurchase plan commit units." The ellipsis drops the entire middle clause naming what triggers the rule.

(The product-scope quote — "Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft Fabric, and GitHub" — does check out verbatim, 2 hits, not spliced.)

Beyond the splice defect, the same Learn doc undercuts the clean 'nothing on the wire changed' framing on substance: ACU redemption is not confined to plain shared-pool PAYGO usage. The doc states "Microsoft Foundry PTU workloads are eligible for both Microsoft Foundry PTU reservations and Microsoft Agent prepurchase plan" and that reservations (including PTU) are always consumed first, with only the *overflow* beyond the PTU reservation quantity drawing from ACU. That means ACU can and does get spent on usage running on Provisioned Throughput (dedicated-capacity) infrastructure — the exact mechanism the register already caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY elsewhere (existing entries #103, #107, #112, #195, all Azure PTU/PTU+Reservations) because dedicated-capacity-vs-shared-pool behavioral identity is the provider's word, not a measurement. An unscoped 'ACU discount tiers = PASS_ABSOLUTE' claim silently inherits that same unverified assertion for its PTU-covered share, which the candidate's reasoning never addresses.

Net: the core numeric/table facts are genuine and unspliced, but the reasoning's supporting evidence for the PASS_ABSOLUTE characterization is built partly on spliced quotes, and the mechanism as titled is broader than the shared-pool-only usage a clean PASS_ABSOLUTE would require. Overturn as submitted; a resubmission should split the two Learn-doc quotes into unspliced separate quotes and narrow the verdict to PAYGO-metered ACU redemption only, leaving PTU-priced ACU redemption at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY consistent with sibling PTU entries.

Quote 'This fee is\ndeducted from your OpenRouter credits.' hits=1 (literal source, not spliced — the \n is a genuine line-wrap that collapses to a space on render). Quote 'same model and provider would normally cost on OpenRouter' hits=3 (Next.js RSC/hydration duplication, not independent corroboration). The verdict tier is correct on the narrow reading: the fee is a post-hoc ledger deduction computed off list-price tables, never a field injected into what the model reads, and the credential swap is structurally content-blind (Authorization header vs. tokenized body — a protocol fact, not a trust-based claim, unlike e.g. the register's own id 164 where cache 'model-invisibility' is flagged as CONTRACTUAL_ONLY because it rests on the provider's word about deep infra fidelity). - https://openrouter.ai/docs/faq — "Usage above the allowance has a fee of `,BYOK_FEE_PERCENTAGE,`% of what the...OpenRouter" with BYOK_FEE_PERCENTAGE defined elsewhere in the same file as the JS constant `5`; renders to "5%" as claimed. This is JS-template-interpolated, not literally contiguous text in the raw HTML, but the constant confirms the figure is genuine, not fabricated.
- FAQ page also has, contiguous: "This fee is\ndeducted from your OpenRouter credits" (1 hit) — deducted from the CUSTOMER's OpenRouter balance. The candidate's reasoning describes this as OpenRouter deducting "from its own credit ledger," which is a mischaracterization (minor) of whose ledger it is.

The disqualifying finding is on the BYOK guide itself (https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/byok, raw HTML). The reasoning asserts as settled fact: "Raw HTML confirms OpenRouter forwards the BYOK request to the named provider using the customer's own key" and treats that as the basis for "everything the model reads is unchanged by BYOK status." The same source contradicts the unconditional version of that claim. Confirmed contiguous (1 hit each):

- "Always use for this provider" appears 12 times on the page as the opt-in toggle required to "prevent any fallback to OpenRouter endpoints" and force "all requests go through your account."

So the source does not confirm "the customer's own key" unconditionally — it confirms the opposite as the default: once a BYOK key rate-limits (exactly the overage scenario the 5% fee is describing — heavy usage above a free allowance) or fails, OpenRouter silently reroutes to its own shared-pool credential against whatever provider its normal routing algorithm picks, unless the customer has explicitly toggled an opt-in setting the claim never mentions. That reroute is a credential AND potential provider/infrastructure swap, not a pure metadata change — and the register already treats provider/infra swapping for "the same" model as FAIL-worthy (existing id 70, "Provider/route selection for an identical open-weight model (OpenRouter-style shopping)"). Net: the fee computation itself, and the successful-key path, are plausibly metadata-only — but the claim's supporting evidence does not establish that "BYOK status" leaves the request universally unchanged, because the same documentation page describes a default fallback path where it doesn't. Nothing here was measured (no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/live traffic per the sweep's constraints) — this is documentation only, so per the bar's own rule ("a documentation sentence...caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY"), and given the conditional carve-out the original write-up omitted, PASS_METADATA is not supportable as an unqualified verdict.

Applying the mechanism lens: the request leaves the customer's machine and hits the live synchronous serving stack in real time — nothing is deferred, restructured into a job, discarded, deduplicated, or billed-at-zero, so the CONTRACTUAL_ONLY carve-out for 'provider asserts it discarded/declined to bill' does not trigger here. Compare to accepted precedent: entries 167-169 and 173 (canonical cache-breakpoint patterns, 1h/5m TTL selection) are also doc-sourced PASS_METADATA verdicts about request-shape facts rather than measurements, so doc-only sourcing does not itself force a CONTRACTUAL_ONLY cap for PASS_SCHEDULING/PASS_METADATA the way it does for PASS_ABSOLUTE claims about internal server behavior.

Also unexamined: whether peak/off-peak is priced by request-send time or response-completion time for a long-running generation that straddles the boundary — a billing-timing ambiguity, not a content/model ambiguity, so it doesn't change the verdict.

settlingExperiment (not performed — no API key, no live traffic this sweep): send two byte-identical synchronous chat-completion requests to the same model, one timestamped inside a peak UTC window and one inside off-peak, and confirm (a) the returned 'model' field and token counts are identical, (b) the per-request invoice differs by exactly 2x, and (c) response content is not degraded off-peak. Where the PASS_SCHEDULING verdict breaks: I searched the full 3.29MB page and the linked official notice (aliyun.com/notice/118555) for any definition of what 忙时/闲时 actually means — clock hours, a load threshold, anything — and found zero. No '忙时指', '忙时为', '忙时时段', '峰谷时段', no FAQ, no 负载/real-time-load language, nothing. The notice itself is a two-line stub (product + effective timestamp only). So the only evidence for 'nothing changed but the clock' is that the same model-ID string appears once in a table with two price columns — that's an absence of a *second* model ID, not a structural argument that busy/idle is even clock-determined, let alone that serving (batch size, quantization, capacity allocation) is identical across the two states. '忙时/闲时' is the standard Chinese term for real-time system-busy status (as in telecom/utility peak-valley billing), not a synonym for a fixed calendar window — and unlike the register's context-cache entry (id206), which is capped at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY because Alibaba explicitly writes 'does not affect reply quality,' there is no invariance assertion anywhere near this note for the candidate to even rely on for that lower cap. CONTRACTUAL_ONLY requires 'the provider asserts identity' — Alibaba asserts a price change, not model/output identity, so CONTRACTUAL_ONLY doesn't fit either.

The closer precedent already sitting in the register is id210 (Z.ai GLM Coding Plan): a time-window multiplier drop with an actually-published fixed clock window (Mon–Fri 14:00–18:00 SGT) — more specific than anything Alibaba discloses here — and that one was rated INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, not PASS_SCHEDULING. This entry has strictly less disclosure than that precedent, so it cannot rate higher.

Request did leave the customer's machine (synchronous real-time inference, not batch/discard), so this isn't the CONTRACTUAL_ONLY discard/dedup shape either. With no measurement possible in this sweep and no definition of the busy/idle mechanism in either page fetched, the honest verdict is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE — the underlying finding (dynamic time-gated 2x pricing on a synchronous LLM endpoint) is real and novel for the register, but 'only when the request was sent changed' is an unverified assumption about an undefined mechanism, not a settled fact.

verdicts.name: google-genai (Gemini/Vertex AI) Python SDK ships with retries fully OFF by default -- the one major SDK studied where the default eliminates the retry-inflicted double-billing surface entirely
verdicts.proposedName: google-genai (Gemini/Vertex AI) Python SDK's own default retry policy performs at most one attempt (stop_after_attempt(1), reraise=True) when no http_options/retry_options is passed -- verified distinctive among the major SDK sources on hand (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS botocore, Azure-core, all confirmed ON by default); scoped to the SDK's own automatic behavior only, not a guarantee against retries an application adds around the SDK call
verdicts.reason:
The underlying mechanism is real and I reproduced it independently from google-genai-src/google/genai/_api_client.py and types.py: BaseApiClient.__init__ sets self._http_options = HttpOptions() (line 719, grep-confirmed) whose retry_options field defaults to None (types.py lines 2665-2667, grep-confirmed field declaration); patch_http_options only overwrites this `if http_options:` i.e. only when the caller explicitly passes one (line 845), so a zero-config client keeps retry_options=None. retry_args(None) at line 572-573 returns {'stop': tenacity.stop_after_attempt(1), 'reraise': True} -- confirmed 1 grep hit for that exact two-line source, and its own docstring says "the 'never retry' stop strategy will be used" (1 hit, line 567). self._retry built from this wraps every _request_once/_async_request_once call (lines 1534, 1726, grep-confirmed, not dead code). No hidden transport-level retry exists: no httpx `retries=` transport is configured anywhere, and the one alternate transport path (google.auth AuthorizedSession) only activates under a narrow mTLS condition still wrapped by the same tenacity retry. I also independently re-verified the comparative superlative beyond just Anthropic, using the SDK sources already checked out in this sweep's scratchpad: OpenAI python DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES=2 (src/openai/_constants.py), AWS botocore DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3 (botocore/retries/standard.py), Azure-core RetryPolicy total_retries defaults to 10 (azure-core-retry.py) -- all ON by default, supporting "the one major SDK studied" as stated.

However, the submitted REASONING contains the exact failure pattern this sweep exists to catch: it claims "grep exactly 1x, verbatim, matching the candidate's quote precisely (2-space indentation and all): `if options is None: return {'stop': tenacity.stop_after_attempt(1), 'reraise': True}`" -- I grepped that exact joined string and got 0 hits; the real source is two separate lines (`if options is None:` then, indented, `return {...}`), not one line as asserted. The same splice pattern recurs for the types.py retry_options field (claimed joined as `Field(default=None, ...)`, 0 hits -- real source breaks after `Field(`) and for the Anthropic constant (claimed `timeout=10*60`, 0 hits -- real source is `timeout=10 * 60` with spaces, confirmed 1 hit). Three separate "verified verbatim / matches exactly" claims in one submission that are false when grepped as literally asserted. The underlying facts they describe are all still true (I confirmed each with corrected, genuinely contiguous quotes), so the mechanism survives, but the specific verbatim-match claims should not be trusted as written and must be corrected before this entry is logged as independently verified.

Separately, on my mechanism lens: "eliminates the retry-inflicted double-billing surface entirely" overclaims scope. What's actually verified is that the SDK's own default retry logic never fires -- it says nothing about, and cannot prevent, an application wrapping the SDK call in its own retry loop (extremely common practice), which reproduces the identical double-billing risk outside the SDK's control. The defensible, narrower claim is that the SDK-level default contributes zero automatic retries, not that the risk is eliminated system-wide.

Control phrase "def retry_args(options: Optional[HttpRetryOptions])": 1 hit (line 562), confirming the fetch/grep tooling itself is working (not a broken-fetch false zero).

Not a resubmission: existing-226.txt (226 entries) has no google-genai / Gemini SDK retry-default entry -- entries #44/#94/#95 etc. cover Gemini context caching and batch pricing, not client-side retry defaults, so this is a distinct candidate.

- azure-ai-inference `_configuration.py`: confirmed exactly 3 sync call sites `self.retry_policy = kwargs.get("retry_policy") or policies.RetryPolicy(**kwargs)` (lines 71/128/185) and 3 async call sites using `AsyncRetryPolicy` — matches the candidate's "3 call sites" claim.

Where it breaks: the claim's second half, "only after an explicit 5xx response," is false as a statement about the mechanism. `is_retry()` (response path, lines 235-242) is:
```
if response.http_response.status_code < 400: return False
has_retry_after = bool(response.http_response.headers.get("Retry-After"))
if has_retry_after and self._respect_retry_after_header: return True   # <- fires BEFORE the method check
if not self._is_method_retryable(...): return False
return settings["total"] and status_code in self._retry_on_status_codes
```
`self._respect_retry_after_header = True` by default (line 95, confirmed, 1 hit). This branch returns `True` — retry — for ANY status code ≥400 that carries a `Retry-After` header, on ANY HTTP method, entirely bypassing both the method-whitelist gate and the POST/PATCH-5xx carve-out the candidate's reasoning examined. That means a POST that gets back a 429 with `Retry-After` (Azure's own rate-limit response shape, and the single most common failure mode against an LLM inference endpoint — far more common than a bare 5xx) is auto-retried by default, which the claim's word "only" explicitly excludes.

This is exactly a case where "the argument holds as a fact about the mechanism only under a condition the mechanism does not enforce" — the candidate's reasoning never examined the Retry-After branch, an unexamined dependency in the same `is_retry()` method it was quoting from two lines below. The timeout-half of the claim is a genuine structural, code-level "no request ever left twice" proof and would earn PASS_ABSOLUTE cleanly on its own; the "only... 5xx" half is disproven by the same file at the same verification pass, so the conjunctive claim as submitted cannot stand as PASS_ABSOLUTE and should be overturned, with the narrower true claim resubmitted separately if wanted.

No live measurement was made or needed — this is settled by source code alone, consistent with "no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no live traffic" for this sweep. token-spread repo was not touched (read-only rule observed; this investigation used only public azure-sdk-for-python source fetched to the scratchpad).

verdicts.name: EEA/UK customers get a 14-day usage-prorated refund right on Claude subscriptions; prepaid API credits are flatly non-refundable everywhere
verdicts.proposedName: EEA/UK 14-day usage-prorated refund right on Claude subscriptions; prepaid API/usage credits contractually non-refundable — CONTRACTUAL_ONLY (provider's word, unmeasured)
verdicts.reason:
Duplicate check: existing-226.txt has no prior refund-policy entry (closest is #212, usage-credit expiry, CONTRACTUAL_ONLY) — this is a new candidate, not a resubmission.

Quote re-verification (raw HTML, curl, not markdown-converted): fetched both cited pages myself.
- https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12386328-request-a-refund-for-a-paid-claude-plan — HTTP 200, 331401 bytes (matches claimed 331KB). "Your refunds will be prorated according to your use." = 2/2 exact hits. "refund within 14 days of purchase" = 2/2. Subheading "Refunds for customers in the European Economic Area (EEA) and the United Kingdom (UK)" = 3/3. Control phrase "refund" case-sensitive = 82/82, exact match to the reasoning's reported count.
- https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8977456-how-do-i-pay-for-my-claude-api-usage — HTTP 200, 323520 bytes (matches claimed 323KB). "All credit purchases are non-refundable." = 2/2 exact hits.
No splicing: each quote is a contiguous substring in its own source; the two quotes are correctly drawn from two different articles, not stitched together. On the pure quote-fidelity axis this candidate is clean — better sourced than most of what's in the register.

Why the verdict is still wrong: PASS_ABSOLUTE requires either a measurement or a structural argument that no request was ever sent — the bar says so in as many words: "A documentation sentence is THE PROVIDER'S WORD, however plainly it reads, and caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY." Every load-bearing fact here — the 14-day window, the proration formula, the blanket non-refundability of credits — comes from a support article and a terms-of-service page, i.e. Anthropic's own asserted policy about what it will do with a customer's money. Nobody in this sweep requested a refund and watched the proration actually get computed and paid; nobody tested whether an EEA/UK customer requesting a credit refund (not a subscription refund) gets the statutory carve-out the subscription page has ("except... where required by law") but the Credit Terms page conspicuously omits (I checked anthropic.com/legal/credit-terms directly: the non-refundable clause has no such carve-out, meaning the "everywhere, flatly" framing rests on the contract's silence on EU/UK statutory withdrawal rights for prepaid digital credits — an unexamined dependency, not a closed question). This sweep has no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and no live traffic (per the standing rule), so "PASS_ABSOLUTE — nothing on the wire changed" cannot be supported for a claim about whether a refund is actually honored as documented.

MECHANISM lens, applied: PASS_ABSOLUTE is defined around "nothing on the wire changed" — it presupposes an inference request whose content is being compared. A refund/billing policy has no wire to inspect at all; there's no request leaving the customer's machine that this claim is about, no key that's content-blind, no routing path to trace. That's a category mismatch on top of the documentation-vs-measurement problem: this claim was never eligible for the wire-content tier of the bar in the first place. What it correctly is: a contractual entitlement/exclusion asserted by the provider, unverifiable by us this session — textbook CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, matching how this exact register already treats sibling claims (#212 usage-credit expiry policy; #191 per-seat pricing as sanctioned alternative; #159 the July billing-classification incident) that rest on the provider's word about money rather than on model-request identity.

settlingExperiment (unmeasured, as required): actually submit an EEA/UK subscription refund request partway through a billing period and confirm the returned amount matches usage-based proration to the stated formula; separately attempt an API-credit refund from an EEA/UK account to test whether local consumer law forces an exception the Credit Terms page doesn't itself state. Neither was done here — no API key, no live account, no request sent.

Net: uphold the underlying facts (quotes are real, not spliced, correctly sourced to two distinct pages), but the classification is wrong by the bar's own explicit text. Narrower correct verdict is CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, not PASS_ABSOLUTE.

The instructions state explicitly: 'A documentation sentence is THE PROVIDER'S WORD, however plainly it reads, and caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. Only a measurement, or a structural argument that no request was ever sent, supports PASS_ABSOLUTE.' The candidate's entire evidentiary basis is a legal-terms page — no invoice was measured, no live gross-up payment observed, and there is no 'no request was sent' structural argument (this claim isn't about requests at all, it's about who pays withholding tax on an invoice). This is Anthropic's own contract language asserting how billing will work, exactly the category the rule caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. The candidate's reasoning tries to borrow PASS_ABSOLUTE precedent from other billing entries in the register (e.g. #24 InputTokensDetails shim, #194 reservation amortization) but those are structural/code/arithmetic facts, not vendor-asserted contract behavior — not comparable.

2. Secondary, on quote fidelity (Rule 3/4): grepping the raw HTML for the candidate's exact 'Gross-up Payment' quote string returns 0 hits, not the claimed '2/2 exact hits, non-spliced.' The reason: in the raw HTML the phrase 'Gross-up Payment' sits inside a <strong> tag, and the surrounding quote marks are the entity ", not a literal '"' — so byte-for-byte the claimed string is not contiguous in either the rendered-DOM copy or the embedded Sanity JSON copy of the page (JSON further splits it across three separate span objects). This is a distinctly named, separately-marketed plan ('Claude Team plan for research labs') with its own landing page and its own pricing table — not a bare credit/rebate applied to an existing account like the Startup Program or the Nonprofit discount (both already PASS_ABSOLUTE precedents). verdicts.name: NVIDIA Inception Program — preferred-pricing rebate + free cloud credits on GPU/cloud-compute purchases
verdicts.proposedName: NVIDIA Inception preferred-pricing rebate on select GPU/software hardware (deducted from third-party supplier invoice) — hardware-rebate mechanism only; the bundled "free cloud credits from NVIDIA and partners" claim is dropped
verdicts.reason:
Quotes check out — no fabrication, no splicing. Verified verbatim (all contiguous substrings, 1 hit each, decoding one ` ` entity): "Preferred pricing functions as a rebate that is deducted from the standard supplier price." / "NVIDIA doesn't sell directly to Inception members, and we don't maintain pricing control over our suppliers." / "Access free cloud credits from NVIDIA and partners for more flexible, scalable development and deployment." / "Members[nbsp]must employ at least one developer, maintain a working website, be officially incorporated, and be less than 10 years old." / "Consulting and outsourced development firms" / "Companies associated with cryptocurrency" / "Cloud service providers" / "Resellers and distributors" / "Public companies" / "Preferred pricing is only available for select hardware and software products and is subject to change." Control phrase "Access free cloud credits from NVIDIA and partners" — 1 hit, page is live and fetchable (raw HTML via curl, 741KB, HTTP 200; not markdown-converted).

But the claim bundles two mechanisms of different verification strength, and only one earns PASS_ABSOLUTE.

(1) The hardware-preferred-pricing rebate is well-supported by a structural argument, not just documentation: it is a rebate deducted from a third-party supplier's invoice on a physical GPU/software purchase. A hardware purchase-price rebate is not a request that could carry different tokens at all — there is no wire in this transaction for a model to read from. That is the same class of structural argument that earned entries 194 (Reservation amortization) and 102/114 (AWS Marketplace private offers) PASS_ABSOLUTE despite being sourced from documentation alone. This part of the claim survives.

(2) The "free cloud credits from NVIDIA and partners" half does not. The source never specifies what the credits fund — "partners" is unnamed, and the page's only description is marketing language ("more flexible, scalable development and deployment"). The candidate's reasoning fills this gap with its own unverified assumption — "a startup then uses to run its own, unmodified models" — which is not established anywhere in the source. NVIDIA's own catalog includes hosted-inference offerings (NIM microservices, API catalog); nothing on this page rules out the credits being redeemable against a shared model-serving product rather than raw self-hosted compute. This is exactly the "unexamined dependency" the mechanism lens asks for, and it is not a hypothetical concern: the register already has a directly parallel entry for this program type — id 119, "Hyperscaler startup cloud-credit programs (AWS Activate / Google for Startups / Azure Founders Hub)" — logged as INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, not PASS_ABSOLUTE, for the identical reason (undefined redemption scope). Passing NVIDIA's cloud-credit claim at PASS_ABSOLUTE while its sibling sits at INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE is an inconsistency the register shouldn't carry, and the fix is the register's established remedy: narrow the name to what's actually proven and drop the unproven half rather than let it ride along as PASS_ABSOLUTE on the coattails of the rebate.

Net: uphold PASS_ABSOLUTE, but only for the GPU/software preferred-pricing rebate mechanism; strike "cloud-compute purchases" and "free cloud credits" from the passing claim's scope.

No entry in existing-226.txt duplicates this (checked all 226 rows; nothing NVIDIA/Inception-related present).

verdicts.name: Ollama keep_alive model-residency parameter
verdicts.proposedName: Ollama keep_alive model-residency parameter
verdicts.reason:
Quote check passes cleanly — this is not a fabrication case. Fetched raw docs/api.md from github.com/ollama/ollama (1872 lines, matching the candidate's "1,800+"). The bullet "`keep_alive`: controls how long the model will stay loaded into memory following the request (default: `5m`)" hits exactly 4 times, at exactly lines 58, 513, 1705, 1824. Control phrase 'keep_alive' hits 8 times total (the 4 bullets plus 4 other mentions at lines 459, 466, 1141, 1149 covering the keep_alive:0 unload examples). Candidate's counts are exact.

But the verdict tier is wrong, on two independent grounds:

1. Register's own rule: "A documentation sentence... caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY... Only a measurement, or a structural argument that no request was ever sent, supports PASS_ABSOLUTE." The candidate's entire evidentiary basis is a docs prose sentence describing intended behavior — no code was read, no measurement was taken (this sweep has none available). "No request was ever sent" doesn't apply either: keep_alive never suppresses an inference call, it only governs whether weights stay resident *after* one. So neither escape hatch is available, and the claim caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY by the register's own stated rule.

2. Precedent misapplied. The candidate leans on entry 45 (PagedAttention/vLLM, PASS_ABSOLUTE) as a "comparable memory-management-only mechanism," but that's the wrong analogy. PagedAttention adds nothing to the client-server wire at all — it's pure server-internal KV-block bookkeeping, and its output-equivalence is backed by a published, code-level/mathematical correctness argument, not vendor prose. keep_alive is a field the customer adds to their own request JSON body to invoke the behavior — structurally that's the same shape as entry 42, Anthropic's cache_control breakpoints, which this register already scored PASS_METADATA precisely because "a field the model never reads" still changed what went out on the wire. By the register's own precedent, keep_alive is at best PASS_METADATA, never PASS_ABSOLUTE ("nothing on the wire changed" is false the moment you set keep_alive to a non-default value).

Unexamined dependency, for good measure: "reload after eviction re-reads the same on-disk model file" assumes the blob under a tag hasn't changed between unload and reload (an `ollama pull` of the same tag between calls would swap it) and that the next request's `options` block matches what was previously loaded (Ollama restarts the runner on load-time-parameter changes regardless of keep_alive). Neither is enforced by keep_alive itself — the candidate's "structural, code-level guarantee" language is stronger than what a one-line docs bullet actually establishes.

Given the explicit "documentation caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY absent measurement" rule, that's the correct settle point over PASS_METADATA — both undercut PASS_ABSOLUTE, but the docs-only-evidence rule is the more direct, rule-anchored downgrade path.

  grok-4.6   → batchDiscountPercent=0, batchEnabled=<absent>

- botocore/retryhandler.py (develop branch): EXCEPTION_MAP['GENERAL_CONNECTION_ERROR'] = [ConnectionError, ConnectionClosedError, ReadTimeoutError, EndpointConnectionError] — ReadTimeoutError present, confirmed.
- botocore/data/_retry.json: '__default__' policy has max_attempts:5 and includes the general_socket_errors policy ref — confirmed by direct JSON parse. I also checked for a bedrock-runtime-specific override in this file (the top-level retry keys are only __default__, organizations, dynamodb, ec2, cloudsearch, kinesis, sqs, s3, glacier, route53, sts) — there is none, so bedrock-runtime inherits the default retry-on-socket-error policy with no service-specific carve-out.
- botocore/client.py: `config_store.get_config_variable('retry_mode') or 'legacy'` — confirmed verbatim (candidate cited line 320, I found it at line 287 on current develop HEAD — a version-drift line-number mismatch, not a fabrication; the code is identical).
- aws-sdk-go-v2/aws/retry/standard.go: `DefaultMaxAttempts int = 3` — confirmed.
- aws-sdk-go-v2/aws/retry/retryable_error.go: RetryableConnectionError doc comment "Includes errors such as connection reset, connection refused, net dial, temporary, and timeout errors" — confirmed verbatim.
- botocore/data/bedrock-runtime/2023-09-30/service-2.json, parsed directly with Python's json module (not eyeballed): InvokeModelRequest members are exactly ['body','contentType','accept','modelId','trace','guardrailIdentifier','guardrailVersion','performanceConfigLatency','serviceTier','requestMetadata'] and ConverseRequest members carry no client/idempotency token — exact match to the candidate's list. StartAsyncInvokeRequest.clientRequestToken targets shape AsyncInvokeIdempotencyToken with "idempotencyToken":true at line 4489 of the file I downloaded — the candidate's cited line number matched exactly. I went further than the candidate and confirmed clientRequestToken appears in exactly three shapes in the whole file (AsyncInvokeSummary, GetAsyncInvokeResponse, StartAsyncInvokeRequest) — i.e. only the async batch-job family, never InvokeModel/Converse. I also checked the operation-level `idempotent` trait on InvokeModel, Converse, InvokeModelWithResponseStream and ConverseStream — none is set, so nothing in the model marks these operations safe-to-retry or non-retryable; they fall through to the SDK's generic connection-error retry policy.

Applying the bar: a botocore ReadTimeoutError fires only after the request has already left the client (it's a timeout waiting to *read the response*, not a connect/send failure), so by the time legacy-mode's default 5-attempt policy or go-v2's default 3-attempt policy retries it, the original request may already have reached Bedrock and be mid-generation or complete. Because InvokeModel/Converse carry no idempotency token (unlike the async job API, which structurally does), AWS has no way to recognize the retry as 'the same request' — a genuine second POST goes out, and if the model already produced (or is producing) output for the first attempt, this is a second, separately billed generation over the identical prompt. That is exactly 'a different amount of thinking happens' under the bar, and it's a structural argument (verified from the wire-format model and both SDKs' default configs), not a vendor doc claim, so it isn't eligible for a CONTRACTUAL_ONLY downgrade — there's no AWS assertion of dedup to hide behind, and the evidence (absence of any idempotency field) argues the opposite. I found no bedrock-runtime-specific retry override, no operation-level idempotent/non-retryable trait, and no streaming-body constraint that would exempt InvokeModel/Converse from the default policy — so there's no narrower scoping that flips this to a pass.

One honest caveat for the register, not a reason to overturn: existing entries #150 (SDK auto-retry-on-timeout double billing, INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE) and #151 (no idempotency key at any major provider's real-time endpoint, FAIL) already cover adjacent ground. This candidate isn't a restatement of either — it's SDK/service-specific, source-line-verified evidence (down to an exact matching line number in the Bedrock service model) that #150's mechanism is real and default-on for two major AWS SDKs specifically, which is new and stronger than what's already in the register. It's additive, not a duplicate, so rule 8 doesn't require dropping it.

No measurement of an actual double-billed invocation was made or claimed — that would need a live AWS account and is out of scope for this sweep; the candidate correctly relies on structural/source evidence for FAIL rather than claiming a measurement it doesn't have.

That description initially looked like it might supply the missing structural-equivalence argument the submitter said was absent (a pure memoization of a deterministic function is provably lossless, similar to why PagedAttention got PASS_ABSOLUTE in this register). Over-restriction would still yield 100% structural correctness while genuinely narrowing the valid-token set and changing what gets sampled — exactly the failure mode the submitter flagged as unverifiable. So the paper's mechanism description doesn't rule out that possibility; it just relocates the same open question. And per the register's own rule, the paper is still the authors' own self-report (same trust chain as the README), so even if it had claimed exact equivalence outright, that would cap at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, not PASS_ABSOLUTE, and CONTRACTUAL_ONLY itself doesn't fit either since there's no metered provider/billing assertion in a self-hosted-library scenario — nothing here to certify as 'discarded/deduplicated but billed as if not.' It's only non-deprecated on the two *response-object echo* schemas (Response, BetaResponse), which just reflect back what was requested, not the operative request parameter. So the parameter you'd actually set to request auto-truncation is currently deprecated in OpenAI's own spec — still functional, just marked for removal. This doesn't change the verdict: deprecated-but-live is still a real, currently operating mechanism, and the question the bar asks is about what tokens the model reads when it fires, not about the parameter's lifecycle stage.

Applying the bar itself: `truncation: "auto"` is explicitly opt-in and explicitly documented to drop earlier conversation items before the model sees them when input exceeds the context window. That is by definition a different token sequence than the client's full messages array — the literal FAIL condition, and OpenAI's own docs say so in plain language (this isn't an inferred side effect, it's the stated mechanism). No narrower scoping rescues it: it isn't misconfiguration (the claim is specifically about the `auto` case, not the `disabled` default that fails loudly instead), and it isn't a documentation-sentence-asserting-sameness case that would cap at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY — the provider's own words assert a change, not an equivalence, so CONTRACTUAL_ONLY doesn't apply either. No request-never-sent argument exists here since the whole point of the parameter is to keep a request from failing by trimming input the client did assemble and send toward the model. Checked existing-226.txt: no duplicate — entry 155 is output-side truncation-retry cascades (max_tokens/output-cap mismatch), a different mechanism from this input-side context-window truncation. Nothing in that register already covers this candidate, and nothing here undercuts the FAIL.

Benefit-list bullets also verify 2 hits each, unspliced <ul>.

The decisive thing the FAIL verdict missed is the full paragraph these fragments sit in, which I pulled with wider context:

'Model tuning provides the following benefits: Higher quality for your specific tasks / Increased model robustness / Lower inference latency and cost due to shorter prompts. Tuning is charged per million training tokens... Starting from Gemini 3, tuned model endpoint prediction price will be 1.5 times of the base model. Old gemini models (Gemini 2.5 and before) prediction price stays same as the base model.'

Three things this context establishes that the FAIL reasoning didn't have:
1. The 'lower cost' bullet is a generation-agnostic description of tuning's general benefit (fewer few-shot tokens needed in the prompt) — it is not a claim about per-token serving price, and it isn't specific to Gemini 3. It sits in the same paragraph as the 1.5x disclosure not because Google is burying a hike under a savings pitch, but because the page is walking through tuning economics end-to-end: training cost, prompt-side savings, then serving-side price. That's disclosure, not bundling.
2. Google explicitly contrasts old vs. new: pre-Gemini-3 tuned models cost the *same* as base model per token; only Gemini 3 tuned endpoints cost 1.5x. This shows the price premium is a stated business-pricing decision, not an inherent 'different weights = FAIL' consequence — and it's stated plainly, right next to the number it changed from.
3. There is no claim anywhere on the page that a tuned model returns the same output as the base model for less, or that the per-token rate itself is lower. The customer explicitly elects to create and deploy a custom-weights model; nothing is substituted silently underneath a request believed to be unchanged.

This register already draws exactly this line elsewhere: id 96 (Vertex AI Provisioned Throughput GSU), id 113 (AWS Bedrock Provisioned Throughput), and id 103/112 (Azure PTU) are all CONTRACTUAL_ONLY despite each being 'a documented price differential for a non-default service tier vs. on-demand,' precisely because there's no silent substitution — the customer opted in. The register's actual FAIL pattern (id 211 LiteLLM Budget Fallbacks silently rerouting to a cheaper model; id 30 Claude Code TTL silently downgrading 1h to 5m) requires the customer NOT knowing the swap happened. That element is absent here: tuning is opt-in, and the 1.5x rate is stated in the same sentence block as the feature itself, sourced entirely from Google's own pricing page.

Since the entire basis for the claim is a documentation sentence — Google's own word about its own price schedule, with no measurement possible or claimed — the sweep's own rule ('a documentation sentence... caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY') applies. FAIL requires establishing a deceptive equivalence claim that isn't present in the source; CONTRACTUAL_ONLY is the correct ceiling for 'provider states this pricing term, unverified independently, and it is not a claim of sameness we can check.'

This is also the internally consistent call: existing entry #28, "cache_read_input_tokens → OpenAI-standard cached_tokens normalization gap in LiteLLM," is the much closer sibling (same repo, same `cached_tokens` field, same general defect class) and is already rated PASS_METADATA, not FAIL. #67 (an Anthropic-side invoicing glitch) and #153 (generic cut-stream gateway accounting) are more distant analogies pulled in to justify the extension: different company/mechanism (#67) or a different failure trigger entirely (mid-stream disconnect, not chunk-shape parsing) (#153). verdicts.name: LiteLLM generic_cost_per_token double-bills overlapping cached and image tokens
verdicts.reason:
FAIL stands — and I found stronger evidence for it than the original submission cited.

Verified two ways:

1) Direct source read (BerriAI/litellm, main branch, litellm/litellm_core_utils/llm_cost_calc/utils.py, fetched live today): the overlap-correction block at lines 841-861 detects when text/cache/image/audio/video buckets sum to more than prompt_tokens, but the ONLY thing it corrects is text_tokens (forced to max(0, remainder)). cache_hit_tokens and image_tokens themselves are never adjusted. Then _calculate_input_cost (lines 654-671) charges `cache_hit_tokens * cache_read_cost` and, separately and unconditionally, `image_tokens * image_token_cost`, with no de-duplication between the two. So when a provider's usage object reports cached_tokens and image_tokens as overlapping (non-disjoint) subsets of prompt_tokens, the overlapping tokens get billed twice — once at the cache rate, once at the image rate.

2) Independent corroboration: `gh api search/issues -f q='repo:BerriAI/litellm image cache double bill'` turned up issue #37281, "[Bug]: generic_cost_per_token double-counts overlapping cached image tokens" — open, filed today, 0 comments (unresolved, not yet maintainer-triaged), citing the exact same line ranges I read independently (654-671, 841-861) before I found the issue. Its worked example: prompt_tokens=100, cached=90, image=80 (overlapping) → correct charge ≈39e-6 cost units, current code charges ≈109e-6 — roughly a 2.8x overcharge on the 70 overlapping tokens. The issue author flags the numbers as synthetic, not measured against production traffic, consistent with this sweep having no live measurement capability either.

This is structural, not a misconfiguration: it fires for any OpenAI-compatible provider whose usage object reports non-disjoint cached/image buckets — which, per the issue and OpenAI's own docs (images count as input tokens and can participate in prompt caching), is a real reporting shape, not a corner case someone set up wrong.

On the bar: strictly, none of the three FAIL questions apply — the model reads the same tokens, the same model answers, the same thinking happens. This is pure downstream cost-accounting arithmetic, same as the streaming entry it was reasoned alongside. But the register already has precedent for exactly this class: #67 (Anthropic ghost-charge billing glitch) and #153 (gateway under/over-accounting of billed usage on cut streams) are both metering-layer defects that overcharge for compute never actually consumed at the charged rate, and both are filed FAIL despite not literally tripping the token/model/thinking test either. This candidate matches that precedent on the merits, not by stretching the bar's wording — I confirmed the mechanism myself rather than taking the submitter's or the issue's word for it.

Checked existing-226.txt for duplication: the only other LiteLLM entries are #211 (Budget Fallbacks silent reroute) and #221 (Headroom prompt compression) — different mechanisms, no overlap with this candidate.

Not a documentation-sentence case (caps at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY) and not INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE — I read the operative code myself and it is unambiguous on its face.

The candidate's own reasoning states the disqualifying fact twice, in its own words: "Nothing about Anthropic's actual bill or the model's behavior is touched -- this is a bug in a third-party observability tool's own re-derivation of the invoice" and "this does not satisfy the bar's literal clause ... since nothing about the underlying Anthropic request changed -- the defect is purely in a downstream cost-estimator." Helicone doesn't bill the customer for tokens — Anthropic does, directly. Helicone's number is a dashboard estimate for analytics/budget-alert purposes. No request left the customer's machine differently, no different tokens were read, no different model answered, no different thinking happened, and — the part the bar doesn't even ask but which the candidate volunteers — no actual invoice was altered either. This is categorically unlike the entry the candidate leans on for precedent (153, "Gateway-side under/over-accounting of provider-billed usage on cut streams") — that title describes a reseller's actual billing of its own customers going wrong, i.e. real dollars change hands incorrectly. Here, Helicone is not the biller; it's a spectator with a miscalibrated ruler. That's a materially weaker and different claim than 153, so leaning on it as precedent for broadening doesn't hold up under scrutiny, which is exactly the situation the candidate itself flags as its weak point ("if that precedent doesn't hold, this candidate might better be described as out-of-taxonomy rather than FAIL").

The sweep's own instructions are explicit: "APPLY THE BAR AS WRITTEN. Do not broaden it into 'a different mechanism decides what gets produced' or anything like it." A downstream analytics tool's arithmetic bug is a further reach than that already-rejected broadening, not a narrower one. FAIL was reached only by invoking a self-acknowledged uncertain precedent to route around a bar the submitter admits isn't met. That's not upholding the bar as written; overturning is correct here.

This doesn't mean the finding is worthless — it's a real, verified, currently-live bug worth tracking somewhere. But it isn't a "changed product sold as a saving," so it shouldn't carry a FAIL verdict in a register whose entire question is whether a saving changed what the model reads or does. Recommend dropping it from the FAIL bucket; if it's kept at all, it belongs as an out-of-scope note, not a scored verdict.

But the FAIL verdict itself should be overturned. The candidate's own reasoning explicitly states: "Same caveat as the Helicone entry: strictly, no model, no token sequence, and no amount of thinking changed... FAIL is applied per this register's established metering-correctness precedent, not the bar's literal 'different tokens/model/thinking' clause." That is a direct admission of reaching FAIL by appeal to precedent instead of the bar's literal text — exactly what the standing instruction forbids: "APPLY THE BAR AS WRITTEN. None of the three FAIL triggers is met, so under the bar's literal wording this cannot be FAIL. verdicts.name: llama.cpp server cache_prompt (KV-cache prefix reuse) — self-disclosed nondeterminism
verdicts.reason:
Verified independently (not the tool that produced the original verdict): fetched raw tools/server/README.md from ggml-org/llama.cpp master (github repo confirmed live: 124,561 stars, pushed 2026-08-18, not archived — load-bearing per rule 7). grep -F on the exact raw-markdown string "the logits are **not** guaranteed to be bit-for-bit identical for different batch sizes (prompt processing vs. token generation) enabling this option can cause nondeterministic results" returns quoteHits=1, at line 580, and it is a single unbroken sentence — no splice. Control phrase "Re-use KV cache from a previous request if possible" also returns 1 hit, confirming the fetch is real and current, not a broken/stale page. (Note: the same string with markdown ** stripped returns 0 hits — the quote only survives verification in its literal raw-source form, which is the form that must be cited.)

Applying the bar as written, not broadened: the question is whether enabling cache_prompt (default: true) can make the model read the same input but produce a different output than it would without the optimization. The maintainers' own text answers this directly — batch-size differences between prefill and decode change the numerical path and "can cause nondeterministic results." That is not the provider merely asserting equivalence (which would cap at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY); it's the provider disclosing non-equivalence, which is direct-evidence FAIL, not a documentation-caps-it case.

Checked the three angles for overturning and none holds:
- Narrower scoping that passes: none — the caveat is tied to the KV-cache-reuse mechanism itself (differing batch composition between cached-prefix and fresh-prompt paths), not to a misconfiguration, and it's on by default.
- Documentation read as weaker than it is: no — if anything the entry undersells it; this is a stronger form of evidence (self-disclosed divergence) than the register's usual "provider asserts identity, can't verify" pattern.
- Rejected for a bad-config property rather than the mechanism: no — applies at default settings.
- Register precedent: consistent with existing entries #53 (continuous batching, FAIL) and #56 (batch-invariant kernels as the PASS_ABSOLUTE fix for exactly this class of batch-size-dependent nondeterminism) — cache_prompt sits on the FAIL side of that same line.
- Not a duplicate of any of the 226 existing entries; #141 ("Provider-native prompt caching (KV-cache / compute reuse)") is a generic CONTRACTUAL_ONLY entry with no nondeterminism disclosure — this candidate is narrower and better-evidenced, but its own conclusion (FAIL) is correct and doesn't change the register.

FAIL stands.

verdicts.name: Self-hosted quantization (AWQ/GPTQ/FP8/GGUF/bitsandbytes) across vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang
verdicts.proposedName: Self-hosted quantization (AWQ/GPTQ/FP8/GGUF/bitsandbytes) across vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang
verdicts.reason:
Checked existing-226.txt in full: no entry mentions quantization, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF, bitsandbytes, or this self-hosted engine set. Not a duplicate.

Scope check: the sweep's own plan doc (docs/plans/2026-08-17-register-sweep-13.md, line 17) states "Serving-stack internals (vLLM, SGLang, KV-cache offload) are out of scope unless the customer runs the gateway themselves." This candidate is exactly that carve-in — self-hosted inference on customer-run infrastructure — so it's legitimately in-scope, not a candidate that should be dropped on scope grounds.

Independent re-verification of the technical premise: no URL or literal quote was handed to me for this candidate (only CLAIM/REASONING/a bare date), so I could not grep the reviewer's exact cited source. I sourced the closest canonical primary document myself — vLLM's own quantization docs — and curled the raw HTML (not a markdown conversion) rather than trusting a summary tool:
- quoteHits: grep for "Quantization trades off model precision for smaller memory footprint, allowing large models to be run on a wider range of devices." → 1 hit, verbatim, opening line of the page.
- Control phrases: "AWQ" → 4 hits, "GPTQ" → 4 hits, "bitsandbytes" → 1 hit. All present, confirming the fetch was real content, not an empty shell.

That source itself states the mechanism's purpose in its own words: quantization trades precision for memory footprint — i.e., it is definitionally, not contingently, a precision-reduction technique. AWQ/GPTQ/bitsandbytes are post-training weight-precision reductions to int4/int8; FP8 and quantized GGUF tensor types are reduced-precision weight formats. A forward pass through quantized weights is arithmetically different from one through the full-precision checkpoint — this is a structural fact about the mechanism (matches the bar's own carve-out: "a structural argument... supports [settling identity without measurement]"), not a claim requiring live traffic to confirm, and not a vendor's assertion of identity that the CONTRACTUAL_ONLY cap was built to contain. The cap protects documentation from proving PASS-side identity; it doesn't shield a mechanism's own admitted non-identity from being read for what it structurally is.

Register-internal precedent supports the calibration rather than undercutting it: this is the same self-hosted-serving-stack axis as id 45 (PagedAttention/vLLM → PASS_ABSOLUTE) and id 56 (batch-invariant kernels → PASS_ABSOLUTE) — both PASS because they are structurally proven to leave output bit-identical. Quantization is the mirror case: structurally proven NOT to leave weights identical. The axis already distinguishes "self-hosted optimization that preserves output" from "self-hosted optimization that doesn't," and this candidate sits correctly on the FAIL side of that existing line.

No narrower scoping rescues it: FP8's "near-lossless" marketing doesn't change that it's a different numeric format computing a different function; GGUF-as-container doesn't rescue it either since the claim is about GGUF's quantized tensor types, not its F16/F32 modes; and uneven per-engine method support (e.g., llama.cpp is GGUF-native rather than a native AWQ/GPTQ runner) is a compatibility-matrix quibble that doesn't bear on the identity question at all. FAIL is correct and should stand.</reason>

verdicts.name: TensorRT-LLM KV cache reuse (enableBlockReuse) — p-tuning input-id collision
verdicts.proposedName: TensorRT-LLM KV cache reuse (enableBlockReuse) — p-tuning input-id collision
verdicts.reason:
Independently re-verified against the raw HTML of https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/advanced/kv-cache-reuse.html (curled directly, not markdown-converted, not routed through the model that would grade its own fix). quoteHits: the candidate's core sentence — "When using p-tuning, different requests may use same fake input ids (i.e. prompt ids whose values are larger than vocabulary size). That may lead to incorrect kv cache reuse, since TRT-LLM could not distinguish these requests only by input ids." — greps as exactly 1 hit, verbatim, one contiguous

block (line 524). Not spliced: it's a single sentence pair from one paragraph, not fragments joined from different sections. Control phrase: "Note that this is the default" — 1 hit (line 521), immediately following "enableBlockReuse=true when you create the KvCacheConfig object," confirming block reuse is shipped default-on. A second, even more direct confirmation turned up independently: "KV cache reuse is enabled by default in KVCacheManager" (line 508). Zero-result risk on either check is ruled out. Applying the bar: this is NVIDIA's own documentation admitting that its default-on cache-reuse mechanism, in a named real scenario (p-tuning fake-id collision, no corrective extra-id supplied — which the docs describe as something the user "should" do, not something done for them), serves KV state computed from one request's actual prompt-embedding content to a different request whose embeddings differ. That is the model's forward pass drawing on content the current request didn't actually contain — squarely "the model reads different tokens [content] than what the current request actually contains," which the bar defines as FAIL outright, not capped at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY. The CONTRACTUAL_ONLY cap in the rules applies to documentation asserting identity/no-change that we can't verify ourselves; here the documentation is admitting non-identity — an admission against interest — which is exactly the kind of source that settles FAIL without our own measurement, consistent with how the rest of this register treats first-party bug admissions (e.g. entries #221-#223, #216) and doc/source-grounded FAILs generally, since nothing in this sweep is live-measured to begin with. Checked for the two failure modes an advocate should look for: (1) scope creep — no; the candidate title already scopes the FAIL narrowly to the p-tuning collision case, not to KV cache reuse generally (plain-text requests are unaffected since real-token extra-ids are always 0 and unambiguous), so this isn't the "different mechanism decides" over-broadening that was previously overturned. (2) bad-configuration vs. mechanism — the collision surfaces under default settings (block reuse on-by-default; the safety fix requires a manual step the user must remember to take), so it's fairly charged to the mechanism as shipped, not to a misconfiguration outside normal use. Checked existing-226.txt: no entry mentions TensorRT-LLM, enableBlockReuse, or p-tuning — not a duplicate. No narrower scoping surfaced that would move this off FAIL. Upheld.

verdicts.name: Agent SDK subagent requests sent with zero cache_control breakpoints (Claude Code #29966)
verdicts.proposedName: Agent SDK subagent requests sent with zero cache_control breakpoints (Claude Code #29966)
verdicts.reason:
Verified independently via `gh issue view 29966 --repo anthropics/claude-code --json title,body,comments`: real, OPEN issue, exactly 7 comments — matches the reviewer's claims. I re-ran the grep myself: 'enablePromptCaching' appears 1x in title, 10x in body, 0x in comments = 11 total, confirming the reviewer's correction of the candidate's misreported control count of 7 (a real self-check failure by the original submission, per this sweep's own rule 3). I went one step further than the reviewer and read the full thread (they had truncated it): KevinZhao explicitly rebutted ashwin-ant's "maybe it's your custom system prompt" hypothesis with proxy-log evidence that ALL subagents lack cache_control markers, not just custom ones — and Anthropic never replied again despite two further pings (MeetMartin, bdoyle0182) over the following three months, the last as recently as 2026-07-29. That strengthens the case that the underlying symptom (subagents billed uncached) is real and independently corroborated, more than the reviewer credited.

But it doesn't change the outcome, because the reviewer's decisive argument is a different one and it holds regardless of how the root-cause dispute resolves: this describes a cache MISS — the model is sent, and reads, the identical tokens whether or not cache_control breakpoints are attached; only the billed price changes. The bar's FAIL condition is explicitly "the model reads different tokens, a different model answers, or a different amount of thinking happens." A pure caching miss structurally cannot satisfy that even if fully confirmed as described — this register's own precedent already rates working Anthropic prompt caching PASS_METADATA specifically because the mechanism doesn't touch tokens the model reads. Per this sweep's explicit instruction not to broaden the bar beyond its literal text, I don't have grounds to push this back up to FAIL. Nor is there a clean PASS-tier fit — nothing here is a confirmed, working, behavior-preserving mechanism; it's a disputed, unresolved bug report with no measurement performed this sweep. INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE is the correct landing spot, not an overly harsh one.

verdicts.proposedName: Subagent resume via SendMessage drops system messages, invalidates cached prefix (Claude Code #86876)
