verdicts.name: Anthropic's own multi-agent token multiplier: ~4x per single agent vs. one chat turn, ~15x for full multi-agent runs vs. chat
verdicts.proposedVerdict: OUT_OF_SCOPE / not-FAIL — withdraw as a savings claim; if forced into the enum, closest is CONTRACTUAL_ONLY-adjacent disclosure, but no PASS/FAIL sameness question was ever posed
verdicts.proposedName: Anthropic's own multi-agent token-cost disclosure (4x/15x vs. chat) — a documented downside, not a savings claim
verdicts.reason:
Quote re-verified independently: curl'd https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system raw (200, 173618 bytes, matches the cited 173KB). `grep -o "agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats"` → 2 hits, contiguous, unspliced. Control phrase "explains 80% of the variance" → 2 hits, in the stated context. Quote integrity is clean — no issue there.

The FAIL verdict is too harsh because it misapplies the bar's own scope condition. The bar's operative clause is gated by its appositive: FAIL means "a changed product sold as a saving." This candidate is the structural opposite of that pattern. Pulling more context than the submitter quoted, the source itself frames the number as a cost, not a saving:

"There is a downside: in practice, these architectures burn through tokens fast. In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance."

Nothing is "sold" here — Anthropic explicitly labels it "a downside" and warns it's only economically viable for high-value tasks. There is no claimed-invariant mechanism (no caching, batching, dedup, or "same output, less cost" promise) whose fidelity this register exists to audit. It's a bare, negatively-framed disclosure that a more complex, more capable architecture costs more — exactly what you'd expect, openly measured and reported by the vendor against its own production data.

The submitter's cited precedents (#67 $16.6M billing glitch, #124 forgotten cron waste, #157 zombie context) don't actually support extending FAIL here: all three are unintentional waste or bugs — tokens spent for zero delivered value. The multi-agent multiplier is the opposite: intentional, disclosed extra spend that the same source ties directly to measured performance gains (token usage explaining 80% of variance in solving hard BrowseComp tasks). Waste-pattern precedent doesn't transfer to a deliberate, transparent cost/performance tradeoff.

This also matches the task's own warning against over-broadening the bar into "a different mechanism decides what gets produced" — treating any token-count delta as automatic FAIL regardless of whether a saving/sameness claim was ever in play is that same over-correction repeating, just with a different candidate. The candidate isn't wrong on facts; it's wrongly run through a rubric built to catch stealth downgrades marketed as savings, when nothing here is marketed as a saving at all.

Register check: no existing entry (1–226) covers Anthropic's own multi-agent 4x/15x token-multiplier disclosure — not a duplicate.

Caveat: this was a documentation/blog-post read, not a live measurement — no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no traffic sent. That's consistent with the sweep's "nothing in this sweep is measured" rule and doesn't itself argue for or against any verdict; it just means whatever label is applied should reflect provider-stated data, not an independently measured result.

verdicts.name: OpenAI Agents SDK nest_handoff_history compacts pre-handoff conversation into summary segments

result.critique:
**1. Shallowly searched axes**
- **apac-providers** (found: 0/12): every provider either had no public per-token pricing or a bare cached-input line with zero mechanism docs. A real pass needs working search (not WebSearch-exhausted-at-200) and a captcha-solving path for Yandex/Upstage — right now it's twelve dead ends, not twelve confirmed absences.
- **china-deep**: WebSearch was dead the whole axis; most content came via r.jina.ai proxy rather than direct fetch, and iFlytek's doc index, Baichuan's real API reference (behind a Feishu wiki login), and SenseNova were never actually read.
- **queue-dedup**: Kafka, Prefect, RQ, Resque, Hangfire were reasoned about from "known design"/guessed URLs, not fetched. A real pass reads their actual source, not priors.
- **contract-terms**: stopped after 4 providers (no Microsoft base agreement) purely on time budget, not because MCA was exhausted as a lead.

**2. Single uncorroborated source**
Google Cloud FSP (one page); Cohere `cached_tokens` (INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, correctly, from one field mention); Zhipu/Z.ai caching (Chinese doc only, English mirror unreachable); MiniMax `-highspeed` claim; and both live GitHub-issue candidates — subagent-resume cache-bust (#86876) and workflow spawn-multiplication (#75648) — each a single filer, zero comments, unconfirmed by any maintainer or second report.

**3. Verdict is inference, not a quote**
- Bedrock Custom Model Import PASS_ABSOLUTE: "AWS never touches the weights' content" was never AWS's sentence — it was inferred, and got correctly overturned to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY.
- google-genai retries-off: "eliminates the double-billing surface entirely" overclaims past what the code shows (an app can still wrap its own retry loop).
- ccusage PASS_ABSOLUTE: "no code path reaches any inference endpoint" is a read of the source, not a stated guarantee.
- AgentCore Runtime "billed separately from the LLM call": inferred from the pricing page's line-item structure — no sentence says it.

**4. Unreachable sources — unverified, not absent**
Microsoft Customer Agreement (403/JS-gated; substituted a different Microsoft page, never read the actual MCA); OpenAI Reserved/Scale Tier terms (403, no Wayback fallback found); the dedicated Vertex AI generative-AI SLA URL (loads as an empty JS shell — a real document may exist there with different terms than the general Vertex SLA that was substituted); Yandex Cloud docs (SmartCaptcha wall, zero snapshots archived); iFlytek's doc index (403). In every case the axis correctly reports "unreachable," not "doesn't exist" — but four of these (MCA, OpenAI Reserved Tier, Vertex genai SLA, Yandex) are exactly the kind of document that could contain a genuinely novel finding the substitute page doesn't carry.

**5. What's still not represented at all**

Two things, and they're the two most common cost levers in actual production LLM spend — bigger blind spots than anything the 34 axes did cover.

**RAG/retrieval cost.** It was noticed twice and explicitly waved off — Bedrock's Knowledge Bases retrieval fees ("RAG retrieval overtly changes what the model reads by design... not a hidden-substitution claim") and the embeddings-rerank axis ("once vectors are already computed, storage-tier pricing... involves no model call, so no PASS/FAIL verdict... applies"). Both dismissals reason from the wrong premise: whether a *chunking/reranking policy* silently narrows what gets retrieved — fewer chunks, smaller top-k, a cheaper reranker — while a vendor markets it as "same answer quality, lower retrieval cost" is a textbook FAIL-shaped claim under this exact register's own bar, and it's arguably the single most-used cost lever in deployed RAG systems today. Zero axes tested it.

**Eval/LLM-judge cost.** Never mentioned once across all 34 axes' worth of notes — not excluded, not searched, not flagged as unreachable. Using a cheaper judge model, sampling fewer eval runs, or caching judge verdicts across near-duplicate outputs are all places a "same signal, fewer tokens" claim could be quietly false, and none of it appears anywhere in this register.

Both gaps share a pattern: they're upstream-of-the-model-call design choices (what gets retrieved, what gets judged) rather than provider billing mechanics — exactly the shape this sweep's per-axis reasoning kept talking itself out of examining.
